Read the output with multiple explanatory variables.

This do-file runs three regressions on the Brexit Regional dataset.
Two bivariate (education, immigration) and one multivariate (both).







regress leave_share share_high_skill

One dependent variable, one explanatory variable.







regress leave_share share_high_skill immigrant_share

Same regress command; add variable names after the first predictor.
Each additional variable is separated by a space.










Element
What it tells you

Slope, p-value, and CI for education


immigrant_share row
Slope, p-value, and CI for immigration


_cons row
Intercept (same as bivariate output)










Education slope (-1.14): expected change in Leave share per point of education, holding immigration constant.
Immigration slope (0.08): p-value = 0.449, not statistically significant.
Each coefficient is interpreted “all else equal.”

title: Bivariate Regression in Stata
text:
Run a bivariate regression in Stata.
Read the output: slope, intercept, p-value, R-squared.
Assess whether a regression result is statistically significant.








Access our Shared Project Folder
Click on data-raw
Download Brexit_Regional.dta
Save it into the data-raw folder on your computer








Access our Shared Project Folder
Click on do
Download regression-brexit.do
Save it into the do folder on your computer








Set the working directory to your project folder on your computer.
Load the dataset.

cd "C:\Users\leona\OneDrive - King's College London\shared-project-folder"

use "data-raw/Brexit_Regional.dta", clear







This do-file is your companion for running bivariate regressions in Stata.
It covers two regressions: one significant, one not.








Last week: we tested whether two groups differ in a mean or proportion.
This week: we describe and test a linear relationship between two numeric variables.








Research question: Do regions with higher education shares vote Leave less?
H0: No linear relationship between education share and Leave vote share.
H1: Higher education share is associated with a lower Leave vote share.







twoway (scatter leave_share share_high_skill) ///
       (lfit leave_share share_high_skill), leg(off)

Each dot is a UK region.
The line shows the estimated linear relationship.








regress fits a bivariate regression: outcome on one predictor.

regress leave_share share_high_skill

leave_share is the dependent variable (y).
share_high_skill is the independent variable (x).










Element
What it tells you




Coefficient
Estimated slope (β̂₁) or intercept (β̂₀)


P>|t|
p-value


[95% conf. interval]
Plausible range for the true coefficient












Element
What it tells you




Number of obs
Sample size used in the regression


R-squared
Share of variance in y explained by x










_cons ≈ 83.92 — this is the intercept (β̂₀).
share_high_skill ≈ −1.13 — this is the slope (β̂₁).

\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = 83.92 - 1.13 \times \text{HigherEd}\]







For each 1 percentage point increase in higher education share…
…Leave vote share is expected to decrease by 1.13 percentage points.
The negative sign confirms the direction seen in the scatterplot.








p-value ≈ 0.000 → well below the 0.05 threshold.
95% CI: [−1.42, −0.84] → does not include zero.
We reject H0: the relationship is statistically significant.








R-squared ≈ 0.30.
About 30% of the variation in Leave vote share is explained by education share.
The remaining 70% is explained by other factors not in this model.








Research question: Do regions with higher unemployment vote Leave more?
Same procedure — one command change.

regress leave_share unemployment









Element
Value
Interpretation




Slope
+0.19
Small positive estimate


p-value
0.655
Much larger than 0.05


95% CI
[−0.64, +1.02]
Includes zero


R-squared
0.001
Near-zero explanatory power










95% CI includes zero → fail to reject H0.
p-value = 0.655 → far above 0.05; result consistent with chance variation.
R-squared ≈ 0 → unemployment explains almost none of the variation in Leave vote.








regress y x fits a bivariate regression and produces slope, intercept, p-value, CI, and R-squared.
If the 95% CI for the slope excludes zero, reject the null hypothesis.
R-squared measures how much variation in y is explained by x.



Why this matters:

Regression is the core tool of quantitative social science.
Reading output correctly is an essential skill.

Be sure to save your do-file in your do folder.













This do-file will serve as your companion for learning how to describe bivariate relationships in Stata.
The do-file covers three types of bivariate analysis, depending on the variable types involved.








Univariate analysis describes one variable at a time.
Bivariate analysis describes relationships between two variables.
The appropriate tool depends on the types of variables being analysed.








Example: Gender and vote choice.
Tools: Cross-tabulation (tabulate) and grouped bar chart (graph hbar).
The video uses catplot; the do-files use graph hbar instead. Output is equivalent.








Example: Newspaper readership and ideology.
Tools: Compare means and bar chart of means.
Use by: summarize to calculate group means.
Use graph hbar with over() to visualise differences.








Example: Import shock and Brexit vote share.
Tools: Scatterplot and regression line.
Use twoway (scatter) to plot individual observations.
Add (lfit) to overlay the regression line.








The scatterplot shows individual data points; the regression line summarises the pattern.
Direction: upward slope = positive; downward slope = negative.
Strength: points near the line = strong; widely scattered = weak.








Open bivariate-bes.do and work through all three cases.
Download bivariate-brexit.do for additional scatterplot examples.
Try modifying the commands to answer your own research questions.








Cross-tabulations and grouped bar charts describe associations between nominal variables.
Bar charts of means summarise differences in a numeric variable across categories.
Scatterplots and regression lines summarise relationships between two numeric variables.



Why this matters:


Describing relationships between variables is the foundation for asking why those relationships exist.
Choosing the wrong tool for the wrong variable types produces meaningless or misleading output.
These skills are essential for interpreting bivariate analyses in research papers, reports, and public debate.

title: Doing Reproducible Research
text:
Explain what reproducible research means and why it matters.
Set up a project folder structure that supports reproducible work.






Being able to obtain the same results using the same data and code.
Anyone should be able to follow the steps of your analysis.
This includes you in a few weeks’ time.






Small changes accumulate quickly, and we often forget what we do.
Clear structures make mistakes easier for you (and others) to detect and fix.
Important for transparency and credibility.






Data: the information you gather to begin your analysis.
Code: the instructions that transform and analyse the data.
Reproducible research separates data from code.






The dataset is treated as read-only.
All changes happen in a do-file.
The do-file records every step in your analysis.

output

Cleaned or transformed datasets.

Reproducibility means others can retrace your analysis.
Separating data and code is key.
A clear folder structure is essential for good analysis.


Why this matters:

Reproducible workflows make your analysis clearer and more reliable.
Knowing how to set up a folder structure now will save you from headaches in the future!

title: The Standard Error
text:
Explain what the standard error of a slope measures.
Connect it to the idea of repeated sampling.
Distinguish the standard error from the standard deviation.








We regress ideology (0–10 scale) on age using the British Election Study.
Slope: 0.017 per year of age. Older respondents lean slightly more right.
This estimate comes from one particular sample of 2,649 respondents.








If the BES had surveyed different people, the slope would differ slightly.
Our estimate of 0.017 is one of many possible outcomes.
How much would the slope vary across different samples?








Imagine drawing 10 new surveys of the same size.
Each yields a slightly different slope: 0.019, 0.015, 0.021, 0.014, 0.018…
The estimate varies from sample to sample.








If we drew thousands of samples, the slopes would form a distribution.
This is the sampling distribution of the slope.
It is centred on the true population slope.








The standard deviation measures spread in observed data.
The standard error measures spread in estimated slopes across samples.
Same concept, different target: data vs. estimates.








A small SE means the slope is precisely estimated (similar across samples).
A large SE means the slope is imprecisely estimated (varies a lot).
The SE is what makes p-values and confidence intervals possible.











Coefficient
Std. err.




Age
0.017
0.002


Intercept
3.84
0.114




Each coefficient has its own standard error.
The ratio coefficient/SE is the t-statistic.








The t-statistic is the slope divided by its standard error: \(t = b / SE\).
It asks: how far is the estimate from zero, measured in standard errors?
A large \(|t|\) (roughly above 2) means the slope is unlikely to be zero by chance.








The standard error measures how much a slope would vary across repeated samples.
Smaller SE means a more precise estimate.




Why this matters:

Every regression estimate comes from a single sample.
The standard error quantifies the uncertainty in that estimate.
Understanding SE is essential for interpreting significance and confidence intervals.

title: Multivariate Regression
text:
Write a regression equation with multiple explanatory variables.
Interpret a slope “holding other variables constant.”
Compare bivariate and multivariate regression results.








We previously regressed Leave vote share on higher education.
Slope: \(b = -1.13\) per percentage point of graduates.
\(R^2 = 0.30\): education explains 30% of the variation.








We can also regress Leave vote share on immigrant share.
Slope: \(b = -0.41\), statistically significant (\(p < 0.001\)).
Regions with more foreign-born residents voted Leave less.








Both education and immigration predict Leave voting separately.
What happens if we put them in the same model?
This is what multivariate regression does.







A simple (bivariate) regression has one explanatory variable:
\[\widehat{Y} = b_0 + b_1 X\]
A multivariate regression has two or more:
\[\widehat{Y} = b_0 + b_1 X_1 + b_2 X_2\]










Coefficient
P-value




Education
-1.14
< 0.001


Immigration
0.08
0.449


Intercept
83.49
< 0.001



\(R^2 = 0.30\), \(N = 139\).







Education slope (-1.14): expected change in Leave share per point of education, comparing regions with similar immigration.
“Holding constant” isolates one variable’s contribution.
Equivalent phrase: “all else equal.”








Bivariate education slope: -1.13. Multivariate: -1.14. Almost identical.
Immigration: significant alone (-0.41), not in the multivariate model (0.08).
\(R^2\) barely changed.








Multivariate regression includes more than one explanatory variable.
Each coefficient is interpreted “holding other variables constant.”
Coefficients can change when additional variables are included.




Why this matters:

Most outcomes in political science have multiple causes.
A single explanatory variable rarely tells the whole story.
Multivariate regression lets us examine each variable’s contribution.

title: Reverse Causality
text:
Define reverse causality.
Identify relationships where causal direction is ambiguous.
Explain why correlations alone cannot determine which way causation runs.








Healthcare spending and CO₂ emissions are positively correlated.
One interpretation: spending more on healthcare causes more emissions.
In the previous video: national wealth may confound this relationship.








Confounding is not the only threat to causal interpretation.
A second problem: we may have the direction of causation backwards.
This is reverse causality.







Reverse causality occurs when:

X and Y are correlated.
We assume X causes Y.
But Y may actually cause X — or causation runs both ways.








Higher emissions → more pollution-related illness.
More illness → greater demand for healthcare.
So emissions may drive spending, not the other way around.








Wealthier, higher-emitting countries may also invest more in healthcare.
But higher emissions may also generate healthcare need.
The data alone cannot tell us which direction dominates.








More educated populations may demand democratic governance.
But democracies may also invest more in public education.
Does education cause democracy, or democracy cause education?








More police may deter criminal activity.
But higher crime rates may prompt increases in policing.
The observed correlation is consistent with both directions.








Observational data show that X and Y move together.
They cannot tell us whether X drives Y, Y drives X, or both.
Establishing causal direction requires more than a correlation.








Reverse causality: Y may cause X, not just X causing Y.
The healthcare–emissions correlation is consistent with both directions.
Correlations alone cannot resolve which direction causation runs.




Why this matters:

Causal claims based on correlations appear constantly in public debate.
Reverse causality is one reason those claims may be wrong.
Recognising it is crucial for evaluating quantitative evidence critically.

title: Reverse Causality
text:
Reverse causality: Y may cause X, not just X causing Y.
The healthcare–emissions correlation is consistent with both directions.

crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

text:
You’ll learn to


Define reverse causality.
Identify relationships where causal direction is ambiguous.
Explain why correlations alone cannot determine which way causation runs.

A familiar correlation


Healthcare spending and CO₂ emissions are positively correlated.
One interpretation: spending more on healthcare causes more emissions.
In the previous video: national wealth may confound this relationship.

section: A second problem with the same correlation
text:
A second problem with the same correlation


Confounding is not the only threat to causal interpretation.
A second problem: we may have the direction of causation backwards.
This is reverse causality.

Definition

Reverse causality occurs when:

X and Y are correlated.
We assume X causes Y.
But Y may actually cause X — or causation runs both ways.

section: The reversed pathway: healthcare and emissions
text:
The reversed pathway: healthcare and emissions


Higher emissions → more pollution-related illness.
More illness → greater demand for healthcare.
So emissions may drive spending, not the other way around.

Both directions may be plausible


Wealthier, higher-emitting countries may also invest more in healthcare.
But higher emissions may also generate healthcare need.
The data alone cannot tell us which direction dominates.

Example 1: Education and democracy


More educated populations may demand democratic governance.
But democracies may also invest more in public education.
Does education cause democracy, or democracy cause education?

Example 2: Policing and crime


More police may deter criminal activity.
But higher crime rates may prompt increases in policing.
The observed correlation is consistent with both directions.

The core difficulty


Observational data show that X and Y move together.
They cannot tell us whether X drives Y, Y drives X, or both.
Establishing causal direction requires more than a correlation.

Recap


Reverse causality: Y may cause X, not just X causing Y.
The healthcare–emissions correlation is consistent with both directions.
Correlations alone cannot resolve which direction causation runs.

title: R-squared
text:
Define R-squared and explain what it measures.
Interpret R-squared as a percentage of explained variance.
Understand what R-squared does and does not tell you.








R-squared is the proportion of variance in y explained by x.
It always lies between 0 and 1.
Read it as a percentage: R² = 0.30 means 30% of variance explained.







\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{RES}}{SS_{TOT}}\]

\(SS_{RES}\): how much the model misses.
\(SS_{TOT}\): how much y varies in total.








Each residual is the vertical distance from a dot to the regression line.
We square each distance and sum them all up.
Large residuals → model predictions are often far off.








Each observation’s distance from the mean of y, squared and summed.
This is simply the variance of y — total spread in the outcome.
It is a baseline: how much y varies without any model.







\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{RES}}{SS_{TOT}}\]

If the model fits well: \(SS_{RES}\) is small relative to \(SS_{TOT}\).
The fraction is close to 0 → R² is close to 1.
If the model fits poorly: the fraction is close to 1 → R² is close to 0.













Dots are widely scattered around the regression line.
\(SS_{RES} \approx SS_{TOT}\) → R² near 0.













Dots cluster tightly around the regression line.
\(SS_{RES} \ll SS_{TOT}\) → R² near 1.








In the Leave vote on higher education regression: R² ≈ 0.30.
About 30% of the variation in Leave vote share across UK regions is explained by differences in higher education share.








70% of the variation in Leave vote share is not explained by education.
Other factors matter: economic conditions, age, geography, identity.
A bivariate model captures one piece of a more complex picture.








A higher R² does not mean the relationship is causal.
A low R² does not mean the slope is wrong or unimportant.
R-squared measures fit, not truth.








A slope can be statistically significant with a low R².
Statistical significance: is the slope distinguishable from zero?
R-squared: how much of y does the model explain?








R² = proportion of variance in y explained by x; always between 0 and 1.
High R² means good fit; it does not imply causality.




Why this matters:

R-squared tells you how much work your model is doing.
Bivariate R² values are often modest — that is expected.
Evaluating fit is part of responsible, transparent quantitative research.

title: Regression Slope
text:
Identify the intercept and slope in a regression equation.
Explain where the slope comes from.
Interpret the slope and intercept in substantive terms.







\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = 84 - 1.13 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

A regression equation is a linear function fitted to data.
But where do 84 and −1.13 come from?







\[\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\]

\(\hat{y}\) — dependent variable (predicted value)
\(x\) — independent variable







\[\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\]

\(\hat{\beta}_0\) — the intercept (or constant)
\(\hat{\beta}_1\) — the slope (or coefficient)







\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\text{Var}(X)}\]

Numerator: covariance of X and Y — do they move together?
Denominator: variance of X — how spread out is X?








If X and Y tend to move in the same direction: positive slope.
If X and Y tend to move in opposite directions: negative slope.
We scale by Var(X) so the slope is expressed in the right units.








For each 1-unit increase in x, y is expected to change by \(\hat{\beta}_1\).
Direction: the sign of the slope tells you positive or negative association.
Magnitude: the size tells you how much y changes per unit of x.







\[\hat{\beta}_1 = -1.13\]

For each 1 percentage point increase in higher education share…
…Leave vote share is expected to decrease by 1.13 percentage points.







\[\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]

\(\bar{y}\) — mean of the dependent variable
\(\bar{x}\) — mean of the independent variable








The intercept is the predicted value of y when x = 0.
Often this is not a meaningful real-world scenario.
It anchors the line — do not over-interpret it.







\[\hat{\beta}_0 = 84\]

Predicted Leave share when higher education share = 0%.
No UK region has 0% higher education — this is outside the data.
The intercept is a mathematical anchor, not a substantive prediction.



















Each region’s actual Leave vote differs from its predicted value.
The vertical distance from a dot to the line is the residual (or error).
Larger residuals mean the regression predicts that region less well.








The slope and intercept are chosen to minimise the sum of squared residuals.
This quantity is called the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS).
Because we minimise squared residuals: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS).








The slope = Cov(X, Y) / Var(X) — how y changes per unit of x.
The intercept is the predicted y when x = 0.
OLS finds the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals.




Why this matters:

Every regression result you read in a paper rests on these calculations.
Knowing what the slope captures helps you evaluate whether it makes sense.
OLS is the standard estimation method across the social sciences.

title: Interpreting P-values
text:
Interpret a p-value and explain what it measures.
Use a p-value to evaluate a null hypothesis.








In the previous video, we tested hypotheses using confidence intervals.
P-values offer a different way to answer the same question.
That question is always: how surprising are our results if the null hypothesis were true?








Suppose we want to check whether a coin is fair.
We flip the coin several times and observe the results.

Null hypothesis: the coin is fair — heads and tails are equally likely.
Alternative hypothesis: the coin is loaded — heads are more likely than tails.









Each time we flip the coin, we ask:

Assuming the coin is fair, how likely is this outcome?

If the observed result would be very unlikely under the null, that is evidence against it.
If it is not particularly unlikely, we have no strong reason to doubt the null.











Flips

Probability if coin is fair

Each consecutive heads makes the fair-coin explanation less plausible.








The probabilities in that table are p-values.

P-value: the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the one we got, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

A small p-value means the data would be unusual if the null were true.
A large p-value means the data are consistent with the null.








Researchers in quantitative social science conventionally use 0.05 (5%).
This is called the significance level (or α).

Reject the null





At four heads, the result is unusual but not unusual enough.
At five heads, it crosses the threshold — we reject the fair-coin hypothesis.








In the previous video, we tested hypotheses using confidence intervals.
P-values ask the same question differently.
These two approaches will never contradict each other.








A 95% confidence interval excludes zero exactly when p < 0.05.
A 95% confidence interval includes zero exactly when p ≥ 0.05.
They are two windows onto the same underlying calculation — not two independent tests.








A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
It means the data would be unusual if the null were true.








The p-value is the probability of observing results at least as extreme as ours, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
P-values and confidence intervals always lead to the same conclusion: they are two ways of expressing the same test.




Why this matters:

P-values appear in almost every quantitative study in political science.
Reading them correctly is a basic requirement for evaluating evidence critically.

Reject the null




At four heads, the result is unusual but not unusual enough.
At five heads, it crosses the threshold — we reject the fair-coin hypothesis.

P-values and confidence intervals


In the previous video, we tested hypotheses using confidence intervals.
P-values ask the same question differently.
These two approaches will never contradict each other.

Why they always agree


A 95% confidence interval excludes zero exactly when p < 0.05.
A 95% confidence interval includes zero exactly when p ≥ 0.05.
They are two windows onto the same underlying calculation — not two independent tests.

What a p-value is not


A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
It means the data would be unusual if the null were true.

Recap


The p-value is the probability of observing results at least as extreme as ours, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
P-values and confidence intervals always lead to the same conclusion: they are two ways of expressing the same test.

title: Confidence Intervals and Margins of Error
text:
Interpret a margin of error and explain where it comes from.
Construct and interpret a confidence interval from a point estimate and a margin of error.
Explain what makes a confidence interval wider or narrower.








Each random sample we draw from a population will be slightly different from every other.
This is not a flaw — it is an unavoidable consequence of working with samples.
It means that any estimate we produce from a sample carries uncertainty.








Suppose we want to know the Prime Minister’s approval rating among all adults.
We cannot ask everyone, so we take a random sample of 1,000 people.
Our sample tells us that 42% approve.
This single number (42%) is our point estimate.








A point estimate gives us our best guess from the sample.
But samples vary, and the true population value is unlikely to be exactly 42%.
We need to know how much uncertainty surrounds our estimate.
That is what the margin of error does.








The margin of error captures the uncertainty that comes from working with a sample rather than the full population.
A margin of error of ±3% means the true value is likely within 3 percentage points of our estimate.








A confidence interval is constructed by applying the margin of error to the point estimate:

Lower bound: point estimate − margin of error
Upper bound: point estimate + margin of error

In our example: 42% ± 3% gives a confidence interval of [39%, 45%].








Confidence intervals vary depending on how confident we want to be.
Most social scientists work with a 95% level on confidence.

We are 95% confident that the true approval rating in the population lies between 39% and 45%.











Sample size: larger samples produce narrower intervals.

More data → less uncertainty → tighter estimate.

Confidence level: higher confidence (e.g., 99% vs. 95%) produces wider intervals.

More certainty requires a broader net.









Two organisations poll the same PM approval rating independently.

Poll A: 42% approve, margin of error ±3% → interval [39%, 45%]
Poll B: 44% approve, margin of error ±3% → interval [41%, 47%]

The point estimates differ, but the intervals overlap.
Both polls are consistent with the same population value.








The margin of error only applies to probability samples.
Reporting a margin of error alongside a non-probability sample is misleading.








A point estimate is our best guess from the sample.
The margin of error expresses the uncertainty around that estimate.
A confidence interval = point estimate ± margin of error.
Margins of error are only meaningful for probability samples.




Why this matters:

Poll results and survey findings are reported with margins of error every day.
Knowing how to interpret a confidence interval is essential for reading empirical evidence critically.

Problem: Using a scatterplot for nominal + nominal variables.
Example: Plotting “gender” (coded 1 = male, 2 = female) against “party voted for” (coded 1 = Labour, 2 = Conservative, etc.).











The numeric codes are arbitrary; they don’t represent quantities.
A scatterplot implies a continuous relationship, but there’s no meaningful distance between “male” and “female” or between “Labour” and “Conservative.”

Correct tool: Cross-tabulation or bivariate bar chart (Case 1: Nominal + Nominal).












Problem: Using a cross-tabulation for numeric + numeric variables.

Example: Creating a frequency table of “age” by “income” with every unique value as a category.

Why it’s bad: You lose the quantitative information: the fact that 25 is closer to 26 than to 65.

Correct tool: Scatterplot + regression line (Case 3: Numeric + Numeric).

title: Summarising a Distribution
text:
Interpret the mean, median, and mode as summaries of a distribution’s central tendency.








Imagine you are choosing a course to apply for.
A university advertises that 80% of students are satisfied with the course.
At first glance, this sounds positive.








A number on its own is hard to evaluate.
To judge whether 80% is impressive, we need to know what is typical for similar courses.
This is where summaries of central tendency become useful.








The mean is the average value. We find it by summing the values of observations and dividing by the number of observations.
It informs what is typical in a distribution of numerical values.
For course satisfaction, the national mean is about 82%.








An 80% satisfaction rate is slightly below the national average.
The value itself did not change, but its interpretation did once we introduced a reference point.
With this new information, 80% is not as impressive as it seems.








The median is the value that divides the distribution in half.
Half of the observations lie above it, and half lie below it.
For course satisfaction, the national median is about 84%.








The median is useful when we want a summary that is less sensitive to extreme values.
The mean annual salary in London (2025) is £70.3k.
The median salary is £49.7k.








The mode is the most frequently occurring value or category.
It is especially useful for nominal variables, where averages are not meaningful.








Which party did you vote for in the general election?













Mean, median, and mode summarize what is typical in a distribution.
They answer related but distinct questions about central tendency.




Why this matters:

Summaries of central tendency help us interpret numbers in context rather than in isolation.
They allow meaningful comparison across cases, such as courses, voters, or income levels.

title: Units of Analysis, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Identify the unit of analysis of a research question.
Elaborate theories and hypotheses for research questions.








Knowing our unit of analysis gives us a foundation by establishing the objects of our study.
Elaborating theories and hypotheses gives us direction by establishing what claims we’re testing.








Are countries with higher literacy rates less likely to experience democratic backsliding?
Are cities with more universities less likely to vote for authoritarian candidates?
Are people with college degrees more likely to support democratic norms?










Are countries with higher literacy rates less likely to experience democratic backsliding?
Are cities with more universities less likely to vote for authoritarian candidates?
Are people with college degrees more likely to support democratic norms?











Are countries with higher literacy rates less likely to experience democratic backsliding?
Are cities with more universities less likely to vote for authoritarian candidates?
Are people with college degrees more likely to support democratic norms?


Country, city, and person are the units of analysis of these research questions.







A theory is “a reasoned and precise speculation about the answer to a research question” (King, Keohane, and Verba 1994:3).
Based on our knowledge and reasoning, what’s a plausible answer to a research question?








Research question: How did countries’ health care systems affect their abilities to mitigate the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic?
Theory: Countries with public health care systems took advantage of their centralised bureaucracies to implement more effective policy responses.


Theories must be reasoned and precise, but they won’t always be correct.








A hypothesis is an empirically testable implication of a theory.
Given your theory, what should we observe in the world?








Research question: How did countries’ health care systems affect their abilities to mitigate the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic?
Theory: Countries with public health care systems took advantage of their centralised bureaucracies to implement more effective policy responses.
Hypothesis: Countries with public health care systems had lower Covid death rates than countries with private health care systems.








Our goal as researchers is not to prove that our hypotheses are correct!
Our goal is to answer research questions as accurately as we can, whether or not our hypotheses are correct.
Trying to “prove our point” is a common mistake at the root of bad social science.








The unit of analysis is the “who” or “what” of your study.
A theory is a plausible speculation about the answer to a research question.
A hypothesis states what we expect to observe given our theory.




Why this matters:

The unit of analysis grounds our understanding by establishing who or what we are studying.
Theories and hypotheses help us make sense of our research question and determine the next steps in our analysis.

title: Normative and Empirical Questions
text:
Distinguish normative and empirical questions.
Explain why we’ll focus on empirical questions.








Some questions ask what should be happening in the world.
Others ask what is happening.
Quantitative social science is concerned with the second type.








Normative questions involve value judgements.

Should income inequality be reduced?
Is compulsory voting desirable?
What is a fair tax system?



These questions matter, but they cannot be answered by data alone.








Empirical questions ask about observable patterns and relationships.

How unequal is income across regions?
Does compulsory voting increase turnout?
How do tax changes affect employment?



These are the questions statistics helps us answer.








Besides avoiding normative inquiries, a good empirical question must meet additional criteria.

Avoid factual questions with a simple answer.
Avoid questions that we can’t answer with data (e.g., hypothetical questions about imagined scenarios.)









Some questions may be important, but too easy to answer.

Which UK regions voted most heavily for Brexit?
Which party governed the US from 1981 to 1992?



If you can find the answer with a quick Google search, think of a different question.








Other questions are impossible to answer.

If Bernie Sanders had beaten Hillary Clinton in the 2016 Democratic primary, would he have beaten Trump in the general election?
Did ancient Chinese explorers visit the Americas without leaving any trace of their presence?



We must save our efforts for the realm of possibility.








Normative questions ask what should be happening in the world.
Empirical questions ask what is happening.
Our exclusion of normative questions is methodological, not evaluative.




Why this matters:

A research method is never an end in itself.
Choosing an appropriate method for a research question is a core analytical skill.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
What is a dummy variable?

A variable coded 0 or 1.
Represents membership in a category.
The group coded 0 is the reference category.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Examples of dummy variables




Dummy variable
Coded 1 if…
Reference group (0)




Woman
respondent is a woman
men


Graduate
respondent has a degree
non-graduates


Dictatorship
country is a dictatorship
democracies

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
section: What can you do with a dummy?
text:
What can you do with a dummy?

Sum gives the count of observations coded 1.
Mean gives the proportion coded 1.
Useful way to include nominal variables in regression.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Dummy as independent variable

The model: Y = B0 + B1(dummy)
B0 = predicted Y for the reference group (coded 0).
B1 = predicted difference for the group coded 1.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Interpretation example

Suppose you regress income on a Graduate dummy.
B0 = average income for non-graduates.
B1 = how much more (or less) graduates earn, on average.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Today’s question

Are women more left-wing than men?
Data: British Election Study 2024.
Ideology: 0 (left) to 10 (right) self-placement scale.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Building the dummy in Stata

replace y09 = . if y09 < 0
replace e01 = . if e01 < 0
keep if y09 == 1 | y09 == 2

generate woman = (y09 == 2) if y09 != .

y09: gender variable (1 = male, 2 = female).
woman: our dummy (1 = woman, 0 = man).

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Your Turn: Run the regression

In the do-file, find and run the svy: regress command.
What is the coefficient on woman?
How would you interpret it in plain language?

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Interpreting the output

Intercept (4.98): men’s predicted ideology score.
Woman (-0.40): women score 0.40 points lower (more left).
Statistically significant (p < 0.001).

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Can we call this causal?

The coefficient is real and precisely estimated.
But does being a woman cause someone to be more left-wing?
This is a different question from “is there an association?”

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
What you already know

In Week 9, we discussed two threats to causal claims.
Confounding: a third variable drives both X and Y.
Reverse causality: Y might cause X instead.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
A third consideration: the counterfactual

Causal claims require a meaningful “what if?”
“What if this person had not received the treatment?”
In an experiment, the counterfactual is clear.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
The counterfactual problem

“What would this person’s ideology be if they were not a woman?”
This question does not have a clear answer.
Gender is not a treatment we can assign or withhold.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Discussion


“Empirical results may be a way to understand what is happening; however, these same data tell us very little about why it happens.”
– Tukufu Zuberi and Eduardo Bonilla-Silva (2008: p.9)


Does the gender coefficient tell us why men and women differ?

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
section: Your Turn: Why might they differ?
text:
Your Turn: Why might they differ?

Brainstorm with your neighbour: what social processes could produce this gap?
If we controlled for those, would the coefficient survive?
What does this tell us about the coefficient’s meaning?

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
What the coefficient tells us

Women are, on average, more left-leaning than men.
The difference is precisely estimated and significant.
This is useful for description and prediction.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
section: What the coefficient does not tell us
text:
What the coefficient does not tell us

Not what would happen if gender were “changed.”
It conflates socialisation, experience, and structural factors.
Causal language requires assumptions we cannot test.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Dummy variables as dependent variables

What if the dummy is on the left-hand side of the equation?
Interpretation changes: coefficients become predicted probabilities.
This will be covered in Stats 2 next year.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
The inventors of your toolkit

Francis Galton, Karl Pearson, and Ronald Fisher built the tools you have learned.
Correlation, regression, significance testing: all from this group.
They worked at institutions explicitly dedicated to eugenics.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Their foundational error

They treated demographic group membership as a cause.
Group differences in health or intelligence were called innate.
This is the same interpretive mistake we discussed today.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Pearson’s conclusion (1928)


“No breeder of cattle, however, would purchase an entire herd because he anticipated finding one or two fine specimens included in it.”
– Karl Pearson and Margaret Moul, Annals of Eugenics, 1928


Pearson studied Jewish immigrant children in London schools.
He concluded observed differences were innate racial traits.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
His own data disagreed

His exams found Jewish children had healthier glands.
He suppressed every finding that contradicted his conclusion.
A public that cannot question data lets malpractice go unchallenged.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Why this matters

The tools are not the problem. Manipulation and poor interpretation are.
Knowing what your tools can and cannot do is just as important as statistical knowledge.
Data literacy makes good citizens!

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
What is a dummy variable?

A variable coded 0 or 1.
Represents membership in a category.
The group coded 0 is the reference category.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Examples of dummy variables



Dummy variable
Coded 1 if…
Reference group (0)




Woman
respondent is a woman
men


Graduate
respondent has a degree
non-graduates


Dictatorship
country is a dictatorship
democracies

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
section: What can you do with a dummy?
text:
What can you do with a dummy?

Sum gives the count of observations coded 1.
Mean gives the proportion coded 1.
Useful way to include nominal variables in regression.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Dummy as independent variable

The model: Y = B0 + B1(dummy)
B0 = predicted Y for the reference group (coded 0).
B1 = predicted difference for the group coded 1.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Interpretation example

Suppose you regress income on a Graduate dummy.
B0 = average income for non-graduates.
B1 = how much more (or less) graduates earn, on average.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Today’s question

Are women more left-wing than men?
Data: British Election Study 2024.
Ideology: 0 (left) to 10 (right) self-placement scale.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Building the dummy in Stata
replace y09 = . if y09 < 0
replace e01 = . if e01 < 0
keep if y09 == 1 | y09 == 2

generate woman = (y09 == 2) if y09 != .

y09: gender variable (1 = male, 2 = female).
woman: our dummy (1 = woman, 0 = man).

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Your Turn: Run the regression

In the do-file, find and run the svy: regress command.
What is the coefficient on woman?
How would you interpret it in plain language?

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Interpreting the output

Intercept (4.98): men’s predicted ideology score.
Woman (-0.40): women score 0.40 points lower (more left).
Statistically significant (p < 0.001).

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Can we call this causal?

The coefficient is real and precisely estimated.
But does being a woman cause someone to be more left-wing?
This is a different question from “is there an association?”

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
What you already know

In Week 9, we discussed two threats to causal claims.
Confounding: a third variable drives both X and Y.
Reverse causality: Y might cause X instead.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
A third consideration: the counterfactual

Causal claims require a meaningful “what if?”
“What if this person had not received the treatment?”
In an experiment, the counterfactual is clear.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
The counterfactual problem

“What would this person’s ideology be if they were not a woman?”
This question does not have a clear answer.
Gender is not a treatment we can assign or withhold.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Discussion

“Empirical results may be a way to understand what is happening; however, these same data tell us very little about why it happens.”
– Tukufu Zuberi and Eduardo Bonilla-Silva (2008: p.9)


Does the gender coefficient tell us why men and women differ?

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
section: Your Turn: Why might they differ?
text:
Your Turn: Why might they differ?

Brainstorm with your neighbour: what social processes could produce this gap?
If we controlled for those, would the coefficient survive?
What does this tell us about the coefficient’s meaning?

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
What the coefficient tells us

Women are, on average, more left-leaning than men.
The difference is precisely estimated and significant.
This is useful for description and prediction.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
section: What the coefficient does not tell us
text:
What the coefficient does not tell us

Not what would happen if gender were “changed.”
It conflates socialisation, experience, and structural factors.
Causal language requires assumptions we cannot test.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Dummy variables as dependent variables

What if the dummy is on the left-hand side of the equation?
Interpretation changes: coefficients become predicted probabilities.
This will be covered in Stats 2 next year.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
The inventors of your toolkit

Francis Galton, Karl Pearson, and Ronald Fisher built the tools you have learned.
Correlation, regression, significance testing: all from this group.
They worked at institutions explicitly dedicated to eugenics.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Their foundational error

They treated demographic group membership as a cause.
Group differences in health or intelligence were called innate.
This is the same interpretive mistake we discussed today.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Pearson’s conclusion (1928)

“No breeder of cattle, however, would purchase an entire herd because he anticipated finding one or two fine specimens included in it.”
– Karl Pearson and Margaret Moul, Annals of Eugenics, 1928


Pearson studied Jewish immigrant children in London schools.
He concluded observed differences were innate racial traits.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
His own data disagreed

His exams found Jewish children had healthier glands.
He suppressed every finding that contradicted his conclusion.
A public that cannot question data lets malpractice go unchallenged.

title: Lecture 11: Dummy Variables
text:
Why this matters

The tools are not the problem. Manipulation and poor interpretation are.
Knowing what your tools can and cannot do is just as important as statistical knowledge.
Data literacy makes good citizens!

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
section: From the concept videos to the lecture
text:
From the concept videos to the lecture

The videos introduced confounding variables and reverse causality.
Today we apply confounding to a real policy debate.
The question: did stop-and-frisk reduce crime in New York City?
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text:
Stop-and-frisk

NYPD officers stopped, questioned, and frisked pedestrians on suspicion of crime.
At its peak in 2011: 685,724 recorded stops.
88% of those stopped were found innocent. 53% were Black; 34% were Latinx.

Source: NYCLU
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text:
The claim

Between 2003 and 2012, police stops increased and violent crime declined.
Mayor Bloomberg and Police Commissioner Kelly argued stop-and-frisk caused the crime decline.
This was their justification for continuing and expanding the policy.
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text: The correlation
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text:
Class activity

Stops rose sharply from 2003 to 2012, and crime fell over the same period.
Does this mean stop-and-frisk caused the decline?
What other variables might explain this pattern?
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text: Class activity
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text:
Police presence as a confounder

During the same period, the NYPD ran Operation Impact.
More police presence → more stops and less crime.
Police presence affects both the independent and dependent variable.
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text: The confounding structure
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text:
MacDonald et al. (2016)

Used a difference-in-differences design (DiD).
Compared impact zones to similar nearby blocks not designated.
Measured the change in crime in both groups, not absolute levels.

MacDonald, Fagan & Geller (2016), PLOS ONE
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
section: How do we know it was presence?
text:
How do we know it was presence?

Bloomberg and Kelly compared crime before and after across the whole city.
City-wide trends (e.g. economic recovery) could explain the decline.
DiD asks: did crime fall more in impact zones than in similar blocks?
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text:
Presence vs. stops

Impact zones saw a larger drop in crime than comparable blocks.
Zones with more stops did not see additional crime reductions.
The effect came from officers being there, not from stopping people.
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 9: Confounding Variables
text:
Why this matters

88% of stops were innocent; 87% of those stopped were Black or Latinx.
Omitted variable bias caused real harm, not just analytic error.
Data literacy makes good citizens.
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Lecture 7: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Test 1: Difference in proportions

Research question: Are countries with a British colonial history more likely to be democracies today than countries with a French colonial history?
Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no systematic difference between British- and French-colonised countries in their likelihood of being democracies.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Countries with a British colonial history are more likely to be democratic than countries with a French colonial history.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Lecture 7: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Test 1 example: Step 1 — descriptive

keep if ht_colonial == 5 | ht_colonial == 6

tabulate ht_colonial bmr_dem, row nofreq

Restricts to British (5) and French (6) colonised countries.
Row percentages show the share of democracies in each group.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Lecture 7: Hypothesis Testing
section: Test 1 example: Step 2 — run the test
text:
Test 1 example: Step 2 — run the test

prtest bmr_dem, by(ht_colonial)

diff — estimated gap in proportions.
95% CI excludes 0 → reject the null.

title: Lecture 7: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Test 2: Difference in means

Research question: Is turnout higher in countries with proportional systems than in countries with majoritarian systems?
Null Hypothesis (H0): Mean voter turnout is the same in majoritarian and proportional electoral systems.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Welcome
Today’s goals:

Review what you learned about describing distributions.
Have a group discussion about the module and collect feedback.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
How good is 80%?

Imagine you are choosing a course to apply for.
A university advertises that 80% of students are satisfied with the course.
At first glance, this sounds positive.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Data in context

A number on its own is hard to evaluate.
To judge whether 80% is impressive, we need to know what is typical for similar courses.
This is where summaries of central tendency become useful.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The mean

The mean is the average value. We find it by summing the values of observations and dividing by the number of observations.
It informs what is typical in a distribution of numerical values.
For course satisfaction, the national mean is about 82%.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The median

The median is the value that divides the distribution in half
Half of the observations lie above it, and half lie below it.
For course satisfaction, the national median is about 84%.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text: NSS Data: Histogram

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
NSS Data: Histogram





About 200 courses between 90% and 95% satisfaction rates.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Interpreting the median

The median is useful when we want a summary that is less sensitive to extreme values.
The mean annual salary in London (2025) is £70.3k.
The median salary is £49.7k.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
section: Another distribution with extreme values: GDP per capita
text: Another distribution with extreme values: GDP per capita

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
GDP per capita: summary statistics



GDPpc





Obs
162


Mean
19,619


Median
12,890


Std. dev.
20,986


Min
596


Max

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Right-skewed distributions

When a histogram looks like your right foot, the distribution is right-skewed.
A few extremely high values make the mean (19.6k) larger than the median (12.9k).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Left-skewed distributions

When a histogram looks like your left foot, the distribution is left-skewed.
A few extremely low values make the mean (82) smaller than the median (84).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Variance and standard deviation

The variance and standard deviation add context by informing us how spread out the distribution is.
This adds insight into how much an observation stands out from the rest.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The variance formula
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}\]

\(\mu\) is the mean.
\((x_i - \mu)^2\) means, “take the value of an observation, subtract the mean, and square the result.”
\(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\) means, “do this for every observation (\(x_i\)) and take the sum.”
We divide it by N to get the variance (\(\sigma^2\)).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The standard deviation

The standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) is the square root of the variance.
More commonly used than the variance and useful to judge how unusual an observation is.
The variance for satisfaction with courses is about 145, and the standard deviation is about \(\sqrt{145}\approx12\).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Interpreting the standard deviation

Linguistics at Glasgow (90%) is two-thirds of a standard deviation above the mean: \(8/12=2/3\textrm{ s.d.}\)

Accounting at Strathclyde (94%) sits at one standard deviation above the mean: \(12/12=1\textrm{ s.d.}\)

The mean and median tell us what is typical.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Right-skewed distributions

When a histogram looks like your right foot, the distribution is right-skewed.
A few extremely high values make the mean (19.6k) larger than the median (12.9k).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Left-skewed distributions

When a histogram looks like your left foot, the distribution is left-skewed.
A few extremely low values make the mean (82) smaller than the median (84).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Variance and standard deviation

The variance and standard deviation add context by informing us how spread out the distribution is.
This adds insight into how much an observation stands out from the rest.

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The variance formula
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}\]

\(\mu\) is the mean.
\((x_i - \mu)^2\) means, “take the value of an observation, subtract the mean, and square the result.”
\(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\) means, “do this for every observation (\(x_i\)) and take the sum.”
We divide it by N to get the variance (\(\sigma^2\)).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
The standard deviation

The standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) is the square root of the variance.
More commonly used than the variance and useful to judge how unusual an observation is.
The variance for satisfaction with courses is about 145, and the standard deviation is about \(\sqrt{145}\approx12\).

title: Lecture 4: Describing Distributions
text:
Interpreting the standard deviation

Linguistics at Glasgow (90%) is two-thirds of a standard deviation above the mean: \(8/12=2/3\textrm{ s.d.}\)

Accounting at Strathclyde (94%) sits at one standard deviation above the mean: \(12/12=1\textrm{ s.d.}\)

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the slides/ directory
text:
This file defines rules specific to the slides directory.
These rules supplement the repository-wide rules defined in the root CLAUDE.md.
Claude must follow both.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the slides/ directory
text:
Slide Density Constraints
These are absolute rules. There are no exceptions, no mitigating circumstances, and no excuses.

NEVER more than 3 bullet points per slide. Adding a fourth bullet point is embarrassing and will always be wrong. If content does not fit in 3 bullets, split it into two slides.
Maximum 10–12 words per bullet.
No paragraph-style prose.
No multi-sentence bullets.
Slides are scaffolding for spoken narration, not self-contained explanations.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the slides/ directory
text:
Punctuation Rules
These are absolute rules. There are no exceptions.

NEVER use em dashes (—) in slide text. Use a comma, semicolon, colon, or full stop instead. Em dashes are banned from all slide content without exception.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the slides/ directory
text:
C-prefix (Concept Video) Structure and Approach
The standard slide sequence for concept videos is:

Title slide
“You will learn to…” slide
Concept development slides
Recap slide
“Why This Matters” slide

Pedagogical approach:

Emphasise intuition first, formalism second.
Avoid symbolic overload early in the deck.
Keep derivations minimal unless explicitly required.
Do not over-explain or anticipate every student confusion in slide text.
Err on the side of brevity rather than completeness.
Maintain continuity with previous weeks.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the slides/ directory
text:
S-prefix (Stata Video) Approach

Procedural, step-by-step walkthrough.
Code blocks should be concise.
Interpretation delivered in short prompts, not paragraphs.
No statistical theory exposition; save that for C-videos.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the slides/ directory
text:
Source Hierarchy for Drafting
When preparing any slide deck:

.qmd template files determine structure and formatting.
Learning goals (from Excel metadata or explicit instructions) determine scope.
Transcripts and prior slides are content references only; do not copy structure from them.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the slides/ directory
text:
Language Notes

Do not describe randomised experiments as the “gold standard”.
Empirical examples should remain consistent across related videos in a sequence.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the quizzes/ directory
text:
CLAUDE.md — Rules for the quizzes/ directory
This file defines rules specific to the quizzes directory.
These rules supplement the repository-wide rules defined in the root CLAUDE.md.
Claude must follow both.



Quizzes Directory Structure
The quizzes directory uses a two-stage workflow:

Quizzes are authored in a canonical plain-text format stored in canonical/.
The canonical files are converted to Moodle XML for import into KEATS (Moodle). The XML files are stored in moodle-xml/.

The conversion prompt used for generating Moodle XML is stored in:
quizzes/moodle_xml_conversion_prompt.txt
Claude must not modify the conversion prompt unless explicitly instructed.



File Naming Convention
All quiz files are named by week and topic:
canonical/W{nn}{topic-slug}.txt moodle-xml/W{nn}{topic-slug}.xml
Examples:

W02_questions-theories-units-variables.txt
W05_correlations.txt

The canonical .txt and Moodle .xml filenames must match exactly (same prefix and slug).
Claude must not add _moodle or other suffixes to filenames.



Canonical Text Format
Each canonical quiz file contains multiple-choice questions in this exact format:
QUESTION: <question text, possibly spanning multiple lines>

A. <option text>
B. <option text>
C. <option text>
D. <option text>

ANSWER: <single capital letter>

---
Rules:

Question text may span multiple lines.
Option text may wrap onto the next line; wrapped lines belong to the preceding option.
Only lines beginning with A. B. C. D. define options.
Every question has exactly ONE correct answer.
Questions are separated by a line containing only ---.
There is no --- after the final question.
Most questions have four options (A through D).




Question Design Conventions
Based on existing quizzes:

Questions are multiple-choice with one correct answer.
Questions test conceptual understanding, not rote memorisation.
Distractors (incorrect options) should be plausible and address common misconceptions.
Questions often present a scenario or hypothesis and ask students to identify, classify, or interpret.
Quizzes cover concept video content only. Do not include questions about Stata syntax or Stata-specific content.
No feedback text is included in the canonical format.




Moodle XML Conversion
Moodle XML files are generated from canonical files using the rules in moodle_xml_conversion_prompt.txt.
Key conversion rules:

Question type: multichoice
single = true (one correct answer)
shuffleanswers = true
answernumbering = abc
Correct answer: fraction="100"; all others: fraction="0"
Question names follow the pattern W{nn}_Q{nn} (e.g. W02_Q01)
Question text uses <p> tags for paragraphs
No stray HTML, numbering, or option letters in the question stem

Claude may generate Moodle XML from canonical files when instructed, following these rules.



Week Coverage
Quizzes exist for Weeks 2-5, 7-10. There is no W01 (introductory week) or W06 (reading week).
Claude must not create quizzes for missing weeks unless explicitly instructed.



Allowed Tasks in quizzes/
Claude may:

Create new canonical quiz files when instructed
Add questions to existing canonical files
Generate Moodle XML from canonical files
Fix formatting issues in canonical files

Claude must not:

Modify moodle_xml_conversion_prompt.txt without instruction
Change the canonical text format
Rename existing files
Create quizzes for weeks without explicit instruction

title: Methods Teaching Resources
text:
A collection of short videos, slide decks, and class activities for teaching introductory research methods and quantitative analysis in the social sciences. The materials were developed for an undergraduate Statistics module in Politics at King’s College London, and are designed to be modular: individual videos, slides, or activities can be reused or adapted for related courses without adopting the full module structure.
Each topic combines short concept videos, slide decks, and a class activity. Concept videos focus on intuition and pedagogy, and are designed to be software-agnostic. Applied videos illustrate how each idea translates into practical data work in Stata. The intent is to support flipped and blended teaching: students prepare with the videos before class, and in-person time is used for active work on activities and applications.
The materials are intended to be adaptable for colleagues teaching research design, introductory quantitative methods, and applied data analysis. Individual pieces can be picked up without committing to the full sequence.
Materials developed by Leonardo Falabella (leonardo.falabella@kcl.ac.uk).

title: Methods Teaching Resources
text:
Browse by topic




Research Design
Empirical vs normative questions, descriptive vs causal claims, units, theories, and hypotheses.






Measurement
Operationalising concepts, variable types, and reading codebooks.






Describing Data — Univariate
Central tendency, dispersion, bar charts, and histograms.






Describing Relationships — Bivariate
Correlations, comparing means, scatter plots, and choosing summaries by variable type.






Inference and Uncertainty
Sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and p-values.






Regression
Bivariate regression: slope, inference, and R-squared.






Causal Inference
Confounding, reverse causality, and random assignment.






Multivariate Regression
Controls, standard errors, and reading regression tables.

title: CLAUDE.md — Operating Rules for the Methods Education Website
text:
This repository contains a Quarto website used to host teaching materials for a university module.
The site includes lecture slides, activities, quizzes, reference pages, and embedded videos.
Claude Code may assist with content creation and small improvements, but must avoid modifying the structural architecture of the site.
All changes should be conservative, minimal, and easy to review.

title: CLAUDE.md — Operating Rules for the Methods Education Website

title: CLAUDE.md — Operating Rules for the Methods Education Website
text:
Hard constraints (do not violate)

Preserve every existing URL. No renaming, moving, or deleting any .qmd file under slides/, activities/, quizzes/, attention-checks/, or reference/. The restructuring is a sidebar and landing-page change only.
Preserve all existing content. No edits to slide decks, activity pages, YouTube embeds, or relative paths inside content pages, except where the user explicitly asks for it.
No institutional branding. No King’s logos, no Methods Centre branding, no claims of official affiliation or adoption.
No marketing tone. Avoid words like “innovative,” “transformative,” “world-class,” “sector-leading,” “cutting-edge.” Use plain academic language.
No career-narrative framing. The site stays student- and colleague-facing. It is a resource hub, not a promotion document.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the activities/ directory
text:
CLAUDE.md — Rules for the activities/ directory
This file defines rules specific to the activities directory.
These rules supplement the repository-wide rules defined in the root CLAUDE.md.
Claude must follow both.



Activities Directory Structure
This directory contains seminar and workshop activities written as .qmd pages.
Activities are designed for in-class use during weekly seminars.
There are no subdirectories. All activity files live directly in activities/.



File Naming Convention
Files are named using the pattern:
A{nn}-{topic-slug}.qmd
Where {nn} is a two-digit week number matching the lecture week.
When a week has more than one activity, a lowercase letter suffix is added:
A{nn}a-{topic-slug}.qmd A{nn}b-{topic-slug}.qmd
Examples:

A04-distributions-activity.qmd — single activity for Week 4
A07a-sampling-activity.qmd — first activity for Week 7
A07b-htests-weights.qmd — second activity for Week 7




Activity Types
Activities fall into several types, but all share the same YAML structure:

Seminar activities — structured exercises for in-class group work (e.g. A05, A07a)
Mock exam activities — practice questions in exam format (e.g. A04)
Catch-up activities — self-guided review for students who fell behind (e.g. A06)
PS2 workshops — structured work sessions for Problem Set 2 (e.g. A08b)




YAML Header Format
All activity files use this YAML structure:
---
title: "Activity Title"
subtitle: "Statistics for Political Science — Week N"
author: "Leonardo Falabella"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
    number-sections: false
    theme: default
---
Key conventions:

Activities use title: (not pagetitle:).
The subtitle: always includes the week identifier.
Activities render as HTML only — there is no RevealJS format.
There is no class: field.




Content Conventions
Activities typically follow this structure:

Introduction section explaining the activity’s purpose
Numbered parts or scenario-based tasks
Interpretation or reflection questions
Summary section listing skills practised

Additional conventions:

Sections are separated by horizontal rules (------------------------------------------------------------------------).
Questions are bolded using the format **Q1.** or **Question A:**.
Hints to students are placed in blockquotes (>).
Instructor-only hints are placed in HTML comments (<!-- ... -->).
Links to the Shared Project Folder and video pages are used where relevant.
One activity (A04) contains R code chunks for generating plots. Most activities do not contain executable code.




Week Coverage
Activities currently exist for Weeks 4-8. Earlier weeks and later weeks will be added over time.
Some weeks have two activities; some have one. This is intentional and varies by week.
Claude must not create activities for missing weeks unless explicitly instructed.



Allowed Tasks in activities/
Claude may:

Create new activity files when instructed
Improve text clarity within existing activities
Add questions or sections to existing activities
Fix formatting issues

Claude must not:

Change the YAML header format
Rename or move existing files
Convert activities to RevealJS slide format
Modify links to external resources (Shared Project Folder, KEATS) without instruction

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
text:
Interpreting your hypothesis test result in plain language.
Discussing causality, confounding, and reverse causality for your variable pair.
Noting limitations of your analysis.

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
text:
Interpreting your hypothesis test result in plain language.
Discussing causality, confounding, and reverse causality for your variable pair.
Noting limitations of your analysis.

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
text:
Introduction
This is the third of four PS2 workshop sessions (Weeks 8–11). Each workshop gives you one hour of structured work time to make progress on your Problem Set 2 submission, with support from your seminar leader.
Today’s goal is to draft your interpretation of the hypothesis test result and to write the Discussion and Limitations section of your report. By the end of this session, all the intellectual work for your report should be done — next week is about assembling it.
You will need the PS2 instructions, the model answer, and the Shared Project Folder (which contains the datasets, codebooks, and do-files).

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
section: Task 1: Interpret your hypothesis test result
text:
Task 1: Interpret your hypothesis test result
Write a short paragraph interpreting your hypothesis test result in plain language. Your interpretation should:

State whether you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis.
Explain what this means in substantive terms — what does the result tell us about the relationship between your two variables?
If you fail to reject the null, remember: this is not a problem. A null result is a valid finding.

Refer to the model answer for the expected level of detail and tone.

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
text:
Task 2: Think about causality
Could the relationship between your two variables run in both directions? Write one or two sentences about the possible direction(s) of causality.
For example, if you found a correlation between internet access and press freedom, could higher press freedom also lead to higher internet usage? Think about whether reverse causality is plausible for your specific variable pair.

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
text:
Task 3: Think about confounding
Is there a third variable that could partly explain the association you observe (or the lack of one)? Write one or two sentences identifying a plausible confounder and explaining how it could affect the relationship.
A good confounder is a variable that is plausibly related to both your independent and dependent variables. Be specific — name the variable and explain the mechanism.

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
text:
Task 4: Note limitations
Note any limitations of your analysis. Consider:

Sample size: Is the number of observations small enough to affect the reliability of your estimates?
Measurement: Are the variables measured in a way that accurately captures the concept you are interested in?
Observational design: Your analysis is correlational, not experimental. What does this mean for causal claims?
Missing data: Are there many missing observations? Could the pattern of missingness introduce bias?

If you are using the BES without survey weights, draft the brief acknowledgement sentence required by the PS2 instructions.

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
section: Task 5: Confirm your Stata work is complete
text:
Task 5: Confirm your Stata work is complete
Your do-file should now reproduce everything you need for the report. Run it from top to bottom and confirm that it executes without errors and produces all the tables and figures you plan to include.
If anything is missing or broken, fix it now — next week’s workshop assumes the Stata work is finished.

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 3
section: By the end of today you should have
text:
By the end of today you should have

A written interpretation of your test result (draft quality is fine).
Notes or draft sentences on causality, confounding, and limitations.
All Stata work complete: your do-file should now reproduce everything you need for the report.

If you have reached these milestones, you are on track. Next week’s workshop will focus on assembling the final report and cleaning up the do-file for submission.

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 2
text:
Introduction
This is the second of four PS2 workshop sessions (Weeks 8–11). Each workshop gives you one hour of structured work time to make progress on your Problem Set 2 submission, with support from your seminar leader.
Today’s goal is to produce the bivariate visualisation for your variable pair, run the hypothesis test, and record the key outputs. By the end of this session you should have all the Stata output you need for your report.
You will need the PS2 instructions, the model answer, and the Shared Project Folder (which contains the datasets, codebooks, and do-files).
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 2
section: Task 1: Check whether your variables need preparation
text:
Task 1: Check whether your variables need preparation
Before producing any bivariate output, check whether your variables need recoding or cleaning. Not every analysis requires data preparation, but some do — and running a test on unprepared data can produce incorrect results.
Review the Preparing Data in Stata page for a walkthrough of common preparation steps. The three operations most relevant to PS2 are:
Recoding invalid values to missing. Some datasets encode missing responses as negative numbers. These must be recoded to missing (.) before analysis, otherwise Stata will treat them as real values. For example:
replace age = . if age < 0
Dropping observations to restrict the sample. If your analysis focuses on a specific subgroup, you may need to remove observations outside that group. For example, to keep only Mail and Telegraph readers:
keep if k03 == 7 | k03 == 13
Generating a binary variable. If you need to reclassify a variable with many categories into two groups, you can generate a new binary variable. For example, to create a variable that distinguishes Reform voters from all other voters:
gen voted_reform = (b02 == 8) if b02 != .
label define reform_lbl 1 "Reform" 0 "Another Party"
label values voted_reform reform_lbl
Important: If your analysis involves a difference in proportions test (prtest) or a difference in means test (ttest), the nominal variable used to define the two groups must be binary — it must have exactly two categories. If your nominal variable has more than two categories, you have two options:

Drop observations to focus on the two groups you want to compare (using drop if or keep if).
Recode the variable into a binary variable that groups categories together (using generate with a logical statement, as shown above).

Decide which approach makes sense for your research question. If your variables are already clean and in the right format, you can skip this step — but make sure you have checked.
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 2
text:
Task 2: Produce the bivariate visualisation
Produce the appropriate bivariate visualisation for your variable pair, using the decision rule table in the PS2 instructions:

Both nominal → bivariate frequency chart
One nominal, one numeric → bar chart of means
Both numeric → scatterplot with regression line

Make sure your chart has clear axis labels and a title. Compare your output with the model answer to check that the level of presentation is appropriate.
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 2
section: Task 3: Formulate your research question and hypotheses
text:
Task 3: Formulate your research question and hypotheses
Write down the following in plain language — you will use these directly in your report:

Research question: a clear question about the relationship between your two variables.
Directional hypothesis: a statement predicting the direction of the relationship.
Null hypothesis: a statement of no relationship or no difference.
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 2
text:
Task 4: Run the hypothesis test
Run the appropriate hypothesis test in Stata, based on the decision rule table:

Both nominal → difference in proportions (prtest)
One nominal, one numeric → difference in means (ttest)
Both numeric → bivariate regression (regress)

Record the key outputs from the Stata results:

The estimated difference or coefficient
The 95% confidence interval
The p-value
Whether you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis at the 95% confidence level
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Activity: PS2 Workshop 2
text:
Task 5: Update your do-file
Add all bivariate commands to your do-file, with comments explaining what each section does. If you added any data preparation commands in Task 1, make sure those appear in the do-file before the bivariate commands.
