title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
Two ideas for today

What are survey weights, and why do we use them?
How can we use plots with confidence intervals to visually approximate a hypothesis test?
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
What is a survey?

A survey samples people from a larger target population.
We want our estimates to represent that population — not just who happened to respond.
But some groups are harder to reach than others.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
The problem: unequal representation

Young men, low-income households, and rural residents tend to respond less.
This means the raw sample is not a mirror image of the population.
Estimates from an unweighted sample can be systematically biased.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
What weights do

Each respondent is assigned a weight that corrects for their under- or over-representation.
A weight above 1 means the respondent’s group is underrepresented in the sample.
A weight below 1 means their group is overrepresented.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
Weights in the BES

The BES uses a demographic post-stratification weight (wt_demog).
It adjusts for age, sex, and region.
Weighted estimates better reflect the voting-eligible population.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
From tables to plots

So far, inference has meant reading a table: find diff, find the 95% CI, check if it includes 0.
Plots with confidence intervals let us do the same thing visually.
This is how results are typically presented in published research.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
The visual heuristic

Each group gets a point estimate (dot) and a 95% confidence interval (bar).
Ask: does one group’s dot lie outside the other group’s interval?
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
The rule of thumb

Point estimate clearly outside the other group’s CI → groups likely differ significantly.
Point estimate inside the other group’s CI → difference likely not significant.
This is a heuristic: it can be conservative in borderline cases.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
Heuristic vs formal test

The visual check gives intuition — it is not the definitive answer.
The formal decision rule remains: does the CI for the difference include 0?
Use the plot to orient yourself; use the test output to confirm.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:

Open hypothesis-bes.do and run it in two stages per test.
Use the plots to apply the visual heuristic.
Then verify against the formal inferential output.

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
Activity
This activity uses the British Election Study (BES) 2024. You will run two hypothesis tests — each in an unweighted and a survey-weighted version — and use the visual heuristic introduced above to approximate each conclusion before checking the formal output.
The companion do-file is hypothesis-bes.do. It contains all the commands you need.

Setup

Access our Shared Project Folder.
Click on do and download hypothesis-bes.do.
Save it to your do folder and update the working directory.
Read through the file from top to bottom before running anything.

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
section: Test 1 — Gender and Reform vote share
text:
Test 1 — Gender and Reform vote share

Research question: Are men more likely than women to have voted for Reform UK?
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Men are more likely to vote Reform than women.
Null Hypothesis (H0): No difference between men and women in their likelihood of voting Reform.


Stage 1: Unweighted
Execute: Run the descriptive tabulation and the prtest command.
Interpret:

What share of men voted Reform? What share of women?
What is the estimated difference (diff)? Is it positive or negative?
Does the 95% confidence interval for diff include zero?
Do we reject or fail to reject H0?



Stage 2: Survey-weighted
Execute: Run the svyset declaration, svy: proportion, svy: regress, and the marginsplot commands.
Visual heuristic — inspect the plot:

Locate the point estimate for men and the confidence interval for women.
Does the men’s point estimate lie inside or outside the women’s confidence interval?
Based on this visual check alone: would you reject or fail to reject H0?

Formal check — inspect the svy: regress table:

Find the coefficient for “Female”.
Does the 95% CI for this coefficient include zero?
Does the formal output agree with your visual judgment?


Note: The coefficient in svy: regress is Female − Male. A negative value means women are less likely than men to have voted Reform.

Compare Stage 1 and Stage 2:

Do the unweighted and weighted results lead to the same conclusion?
If the estimates differ, which direction does the weighting move them?
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
Test 2 — Newspaper readership and ideology

Research question: Are Telegraph readers more right-leaning than Daily Mail readers?
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Telegraph readers are more right-leaning than Mail readers.
Null Hypothesis (H0): No difference in mean ideology between Mail and Telegraph readers.


Stage 1: Unweighted
Execute: Run the descriptive summary and the ttest command.
Interpret:

What is the mean ideology score for Mail readers? For Telegraph readers?
What is the estimated difference (diff)? Which group is further right?
Does the 95% confidence interval for diff include zero?
Do we reject or fail to reject H0?



Stage 2: Survey-weighted
Execute: Run the svyset declaration, svy: mean, svy: regress, and the marginsplot commands.
Visual heuristic — inspect the plot:

Locate the point estimate for Daily Mail readers and the confidence interval for Telegraph readers.
Does the Mail point estimate lie inside or outside the Telegraph confidence interval?
Based on this visual check alone: would you reject or fail to reject H0?

Formal check — inspect the svy: regress table:

Find the coefficient for the Telegraph group.
Does the 95% CI for this coefficient include zero?
Does the formal output agree with your visual judgment?


Note: The coefficient in svy: regress is Telegraph − Mail. A positive value means Telegraph readers place themselves further right than Mail readers on average.

Compare Stage 1 and Stage 2:

Do the unweighted and weighted results lead to the same conclusion?
This example is chosen deliberately: the result does not change dramatically. What does this tell us about when weights matter most?
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Weights and Visual Inference
text:
Summary
In this activity, you have:

Applied survey weights using svyset and svy: commands to produce design-corrected estimates.
Used a marginsplot to visually approximate whether two groups differ significantly.
Practised the rule of thumb: a point estimate lying outside the other group’s CI is a signal of a likely significant difference.
Verified visual judgments against the formal confidence interval for the difference.

The visual heuristic is a practical skill for reading published research. The formal test remains the definitive check.

title: Activity: Data Handling to Bivariate Interpretation
text:
Introduction
This activity is designed for students who either did not attend their seminars on Week 5 or attended but found the bivariate correlations activity challenging. It helps you learn the foundational skills you will need for the second half of the module, when we move into hypothesis testing and statistical inference.
The activity has three parts:

Setting up your workflow — Confirming that your folder structure is in place and that you can load a dataset in Stata.
Describing single variables — Reviewing variable types and univariate description.
Describing relationships between variables — Producing and interpreting bivariate output.

If you are comfortable with Parts 1 or 2, feel free to skip ahead. If you’re in doubt on whether you’re comfortable or not, give them a try.
Completing all three parts should take approximately 90 minutes. If you cannot complete this activity independently, book an appointment with me by clicking here.
crumbs: Activity: Data Handling to Bivariate Interpretation

title: Activity: Data Handling to Bivariate Interpretation
text:
Part 1: Setting Up Your Workflow
This part confirms that you can navigate the folder structure, set the working directory, and load a dataset in Stata. If you completed the Week 2 seminar activities (Parts 1 and 2) successfully, this should be straightforward. If not, work through each step carefully.
If you get stuck, review:

Doing Reproducible Research (also on Keats)
The Stata Interface (Setting the Working Directory) (Keats)
Loading and Browsing Data (Keats)


Locate your project folder
You should have created a folder called my-research-project/ (or a different name you may have chosen). This folder should contain four subfolders:

data-raw
data-clean
do
output

Open your file explorer (Windows) or Finder (Mac) and locate this folder. Confirm that all four subfolders are present.
If you cannot find this folder, you need to set it up now. Review the Doing Reproducible Research video (also on Keats) and create the folder structure as instructed.


Download the dataset
We will use the Quality of Government (QoG) dataset for this activity.

Go to our Shared Project Folder.
Click on the data-raw folder.
Download Quality_of_Government_2026.dta.
Save it into your local data-raw folder.



Set the working directory
Before you can load data in Stata, you need to tell Stata where your project folder is located. This is called setting the working directory.

Open Stata.
Go to File > Change working directory.
Navigate to your my-research-project/ folder and select it.
After you click “OK”, look at the Command History pane on the left-hand side. You should see a command that starts with cd followed by the path to your folder.

If you need a reminder, review the The Stata Interface video (also on Keats), which walks through this process step-by-step.


Save the working directory command
You should have a file called set-wd.do in your do folder from Week 3. This file contains the command that sets your working directory. It serves as a reference so you can copy-paste the command that sets the working directory. This way, you don’t have to use the menu every time.

In Stata, right-click on the command in the Command History pane that starts with cd.
Click “Copy”.
Open the Do-file Editor by clicking the icon that looks like a sheet of paper with a pencil.
Paste the command into a new do-file.
Save this do-file as set-wd.do in your do folder.

If you already have set-wd.do from Week 3: Open it and confirm that the path matches your current folder location.


Load the dataset
Now that the working directory is set, you can load the QoG dataset.

Open a new do-file in Stata (click the Do-file Editor icon).
On the first line, copy and paste the cd command from your set-wd.do file.
On the second line, type: use "data-raw/Quality_of_Government_2026.dta", clear
Click the “Execute (do)” button (the icon that looks like a sheet of paper with a play button).

If you see an error message, check that:

You have saved Quality_of_Government_2026.dta in your local data-raw folder.
The working directory is set to my-research-project/.
You have spelled the dataset name exactly as shown (including the file extension .dta).

If you are still stuck, note the exact error message and bring it to office hours.
If you need a reminder: Review the Loading and Browsing Data video (also on Keats).


Save your do-file
Save this do-file in your do folder as reading-week-catchup.do. You will continue adding commands to this file as you work through Parts 2 and 3.


Summary of Part 1
You should now have:

A folder structure in place with four subfolders.
The QoG dataset downloaded and saved in your local data-raw folder.
A do-file that sets the working directory and loads the dataset.
Confirmation that the dataset appears in the Variables pane when you run your do-file.

If any of these steps did not work, book an office hour.

title: Activity: Data Handling to Bivariate Interpretation
text:
Part 2: Describing Single Variables
Before you can describe relationships between variables, you need to be able to describe individual variables. This part reviews variable types and univariate description.
If you get stuck, review:

Summarising a Distribution (Keats)
Summarising Distributions in Stata (Keats)


Identify variable types
The QoG dataset contains many variables. We will focus on three variables that you encountered in Week 5:

gol_est — Electoral system type (1 = Majoritarian, 2 = Proportional, 3 = Mixed)
wdi_gini — Gini index (a measure of income inequality, ranging from 0 to 100)
ti_cpi — Corruption Perceptions Index (ranging from 0 = highly corrupt to 100 = highly clean)

Before continuing: Download the QoG Codebook from the Shared Project Folder and open it. Use the codebook to confirm the descriptions of these three variables.
Check: Answer these questions before moving on:

What type of variable is gol_est? (Nominal, ordinal, or numeric?)
What type of variable is wdi_gini? (Nominal, ordinal, or numeric?)
What type of variable is ti_cpi? (Nominal, ordinal, or numeric?)


Hint: A variable is not necessarily numeric just because it is coded with numbers. gol_est is coded as 1, 2, and 3, but what do these numbers represent? Are they meaningful quantities, or are they labels for categories?

If you are uncertain: Review the Types of Variables video (also on Keats) before proceeding.


Describe a nominal variable
For nominal variables, we summarize them using frequency tables. A frequency table shows how many observations fall into each category.

Add the following command to your do-file: tab gol_est
Run the command (select it and click “execute/do”).
Look at the results. You should see a table showing how many countries have each type of electoral system.

Check:

How many countries in the dataset have majoritarian electoral systems?
How many have proportional systems?
How many have mixed systems?



Describe a numeric variable
For numeric variables, we summarize them using summary statistics such as the mean, median, minimum, and maximum.

Add the following command to your do-file: summarize wdi_gini
Run the command (select it and click “execute/do”).
Look at the results. You should see a table with five columns: variable name, observations, mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum.

Check:

What is the mean value of the Gini index across all countries in the dataset?
What is the minimum value? What is the maximum value?
What does this range tell you about variation in income inequality across countries?

If you need a reminder about summary statistics: Review the Summarising a Distribution video (also on Keats).


Summary of Part 2
You should now be able to:

Identify whether a variable is nominal, ordinal, or numeric.
Produce a frequency table for a nominal variable.
Produce summary statistics for a numeric variable.

If you struggled with any of these tasks, revisit the relevant videos before moving to Part 3.
crumbs: Activity: Data Handling to Bivariate Interpretation

title: Activity: Data Handling to Bivariate Interpretation
text:
Part 3: Describing Relationships Between Variables
In this part, you will produce and interpret bivariate output. You will work through two variable pairs that represent two of the three analytical cases from Week 5.
Reference material: You can download the bivariate-qog.do file from the Shared Project Folder (in the do subfolder) to see worked examples of all the commands used in this section. Open this file in Stata and inspect how the commands are structured.
If you get stuck, review:

Comparing Means by Category (Keats)
Scatterplots and Regression Lines (Keats)
From Variable Types to Plots and Tables (Keats)
Describing Correlations in Stata (Keats)


Review the analytical cases
In Week 5, you learned that the appropriate bivariate tool depends on the types of variables you are analyzing:

Case 1: Both variables are nominal → cross-tabulation and bivariate bar chart
Case 2: One nominal, one numeric → compare means and bar chart of means
Case 3: Both numeric → scatterplot and regression line

If you need a reminder: Review the From Variable Types to Plots and Tables video (also on Keats).


Pair 1 — Electoral system and voter turnout (Case 2)
We will analyze the relationship between electoral system type (gol_est) and voter turnout (ideavt_legvt). Check the codebook to confirm what ideavt_legvt measures.
Check:

What type of variable is gol_est? (You answered this in Part 2.)
What type of variable is ideavt_legvt?
Which analytical case does this pair belong to? (Case 1, Case 2, or Case 3?)


Compare means across groups
To compare the mean turnout for each electoral system type, we use the sort and by commands together.

Add these two commands to your do-file:

sort gol_est
by gol_est: summarize ideavt_legvt

Run the commands (select them and click “execute/do”).
Look at the results. You should see separate summary statistics for each electoral system type.

Interpret the output:

Which electoral system type has the highest mean turnout?
Which has the lowest mean turnout?
Is the difference between them large or small?



Visualize the relationship
A bar chart of means makes the comparison easier to see.

Add the following command to your do-file: graph hbar ideavt_legvt, over(gol_est)
Run the command (select the command and click “execute/do”).
A bar chart should appear in a new window.

Check:

Does the visual pattern match what you saw in the summary statistics?
Is the difference between electoral system types visually clear, or are the bars similar in height?




Pair 2 — Inequality and corruption (Case 3)
We will analyze the relationship between income inequality (wdi_gini) and perceived corruption (ti_cpi). Check the codebook to confirm what ti_cpi measures. Pay close attention to the direction of the scale: does a higher score mean more corruption or less corruption?
Check

What type of variable is wdi_gini?
What type of variable is ti_cpi?
Which analytical case does this pair belong to? (Case 1, Case 2, or Case 3?)


Create a scatterplot with regression line

Add the following command to your do-file: twoway (scatter ti_cpi wdi_gini) (lfit ti_cpi wdi_gini), leg(off)
Run the command.
A scatterplot with a regression line should appear in a new window.

If you need a reminder about scatterplots: Review the Scatterplots and Regression Lines video (also on Keats).


Interpret the scatterplot

Does the regression line slope upward or downward?
Remember that higher ti_cpi scores mean less corruption. What does the slope tell you about the relationship between inequality and corruption?
Are the points tightly clustered around the regression line, or are they widely scattered?

Write your interpretation in complete sentences. For example: “The regression line slopes [upward/downward], which means that countries with higher levels of income inequality tend to have [higher/lower] levels of perceived corruption.”

Hint: Getting the direction of the ti_cpi scale right is essential. Confirm which end of the scale represents more corruption before interpreting the slope.




Summary of Part 3
You should now be able to:

Determine which analytical case applies to a given pair of variables.
Compare means across groups using sort and by: summarize.
Produce a bar chart of means for a nominal × numeric pair.
Produce a scatterplot with a regression line for a numeric × numeric pair.
Interpret the output in substantive terms.

Introduction
In this activity, you will practice interpreting histograms, understanding the relationship between distribution shape and summary statistics, and performing manual calculations. Work through the sections in order, discussing your answers with your group before moving on.

title: Activity: Describing Distributions
text:
Part 1: Interpreting Histograms
Below are three histograms representing different distributions. For each histogram, answer the interpretation questions that follow.

Distribution A









Questions:

Approximately how many observations fall between 40 and 60?
Is this distribution symmetric, right-skewed, or left-skewed?
Where is most of the mass concentrated?



Distribution B









Questions:

Approximately how many observations fall between 0 and 20?
Is this distribution symmetric, right-skewed, or left-skewed?
Are there any extreme values? If so, in which direction?

title: Activity: Describing Distributions
section: Part 2: Skewness and Mean vs Median
text:
Part 2: Skewness and Mean vs Median
In this section, you will examine two clearly skewed distributions and predict the relationship between the mean and median based on the shape of the histogram.

Right-Skewed Distribution









Questions:

In this distribution, would you expect the mean to be larger or smaller than the median?
Why? Explain your reasoning in terms of the shape of the distribution and the location of extreme values.



Left-Skewed Distribution









Questions:

In this distribution, would you expect the mean to be larger or smaller than the median?
Why? Explain your reasoning in terms of the shape of the distribution and the location of extreme values.

title: Activity: Describing Distributions
text:
Part 3: Manual Calculation Exercise
These calculations won’t be in the exam, but we want you to learn them.
Consider the following dataset, which represents the number of years of education for five respondents:
Years of Education: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18
Using these five observations, calculate the following by hand (you may use a calculator for arithmetic):

The mean
The median
The variance (use the formula: \(\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}\))
The standard deviation (the square root of the variance)

Show your work for each calculation.

title: Activity: Describing Distributions
text:
Reflection Questions
After completing the activity, discuss the following questions with your group:

How does the shape of a distribution (symmetric, right-skewed, left-skewed) affect the relationship between the mean and the median?
Why is the standard deviation useful for understanding how unusual an observation is?
In what types of real-world political or social data would you expect to see right-skewed distributions? Left-skewed distributions?

text:
Summary
In this activity, you have:

Interpreted histograms to identify shape, central tendency, and spread.
Connected the shape of a distribution to the relationship between mean and median.
Performed manual calculations of key summary statistics.

These skills are foundational for describing data and understanding what patterns mean in political science research.

title: Activity: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Introduction
In research, it can be tempting to jump straight to “testing something” without being clear about what you are asking, what explanation you find plausible, and what you would expect to observe if that explanation were correct.
This activity gives you a simple workflow that you will use repeatedly in this module:
research question → theory → hypothesis

Activity: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses

title: Activity: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Overview

Descriptive questions ask what the world looks like. They describe distributions, trends, or correlations.
Causal questions ask what would happen if we intervened. They ask whether changing one thing would change another.
A theory is a reasoned and precise speculation about the answer to a research question.
A hypothesis is an empirically testable implication of a theory: given your theory, what should we observe in the world?

title: Activity: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Examples

Descriptive vs causal
Descriptive questions:

What percentage of countries are democratic?
Is there a global trend towards democratic backsliding?
Is democratic backsliding more prevalent in countries with higher political polarisation?

Causal questions:

Does exposure to divisive content on social media make people more tolerant of political violence?
Does declining trust in political elites weaken commitment to democratic norms?
Do compulsory voting laws increase political participation?



From theory to hypothesis

Research question: How did countries’ health care systems affect their abilities to mitigate the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic?
Theory: Countries with public health care systems took advantage of their centralised bureaucracies to implement more effective policy responses.
Hypothesis: Countries with public health care systems had lower Covid death rates than countries with private health care systems.

title: Activity: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Tasks
Work in groups of about three. Your goal is to produce one coherent chain consisting of a research question, a classification (descriptive/causal), one theory, and one hypothesis.

1. Formulate a research question

Write one empirical research question about a social or political phenomenon.
Your question should be answerable in principle with data (even if you do not yet know what data you would use).



2. Classify your question

Is your question descriptive or causal? Write one sentence explaining why.



3. State one theory

Write one theory: a reasoned and precise speculation about the answer to your research question.
The theory should explain why (not just restate the question).



4. Derive one hypothesis

Write one hypothesis implied by your theory.
The hypothesis should be empirically testable and should make clear what you would expect to observe in the world.

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text: Discussing the differences between quantitative and qualitative research in the social sciences.

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Introduction
Quantitative research shares certain norms and objectives that other approaches may not have. However, we do not want to convey the message that qualitative approaches are inferior. They are just not the focus of this module.

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Overview
The table below summarises a section of a widely read paper by Mahoney and Goertz (2006).1







Quantitative
Qualitative




Concerned with the average effect of one or more causes across cases.
Concerned with specific outcomes in particular cases.


Interested in general, lawlike statements about causal effects.
Less concerned with generalisation.


“What is the effect of economic development on democracy?”
“Did economic development contribute to Spain’s transition to democracy?”


“What effect does a given increase in foreign direct investment have on economic growth?”
“Were high levels of foreign investment a sufficient explanation for the economic miracle in South Korea?”

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Examples
Suppose you are interested in studying the relationship between economic development and democratisation. You are conflicted between two approaches to your research topic:

Example of quantitative research

Assemble a dataset with as many countries as possible, with information on GDP per capita (independent variable), level of democracy (dependent variable), and other quantifiable variables that may relate to democratisation.
Conduct a statistical analysis of the data, analysing whether more developed countries are, on average, more democratic than less developed countries.



Example of qualitative research

Select one or more cases of transition to democracy (e.g., Spain 1975, Brazil 1985, Poland 1989.)
In each case, analyse historical archives (e.g., news articles, government memos, pamphlets, letters) and interview political elites involved in the democratization process.
Assess whether democratisation, in these cases, can be traced back to economic development.

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Pros and Cons
In your group, discuss: what are the pros and cons of each approach? What do we gain and what do we miss when we choose them?
Work with your peers to fill out the two-by-two table below. Try to think of at least one advantage and one disadvantage for each approach:




Pros
Cons




Quantitative




Qualitative





After the group discussion, we will reconvene and share our insights with the class.

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Mixed Methods
Quantitative and qualitative approaches have advantages and disadvantages in a way that they may complement each other. In fact, mixed-method approaches2 are increasingly common in the social sciences. In this course, however, we will focus on quantitative research. It is important to reflect on what it can and cannot do.

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Beyond Causation
The goal of causation is shared by a lot of the research in social science, but it is not universal. Research can have other goals beyond studying if A causes B. For example, Schaffer (1998)3 studies how people in Senegal understand democratic institutions and political concepts. What does democracy even mean for the Senegalese? Schaffer finds that people in Senegal see voting more as a matter of reinforcing community ties than of choosing leaders. This is an important study that used qualitative research methods.

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Summary
In this activity, you have:

Compared the goals and methods of quantitative and qualitative research.
Identified advantages and disadvantages of each approach.
Recognised that mixed-method approaches can combine the strengths of both traditions.

title: Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Footnotes


Mahoney, James, and Gary Goertz. “A Tale of Two Cultures: Contrasting Quantitative and Qualitative Research.” Political Analysis 14, no. 3 (2006): 227–49. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpj017.↩︎
For a comprehensive review, see: Seawright, Jason. Multi-Method Social Science: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Tools. Cambridge University Press, 2016.↩︎
Schaffer, Frederic Charles. Democracy in Translation: Understanding Politics in an Unfamiliar Culture. The Wilder House Series in Politics, History, and Culture. Ithaca, N.Y: Cornell University Press, 1998.↩︎

title: Activity: Proposing Measurement Strategies
text:
Introduction
Hypothesis: Countries with higher levels of education are more likely to be democratic than countries with lower levels of education.
How should we measure the level of education? What information should we rely on to determine whether Mexico is more or less educated than Colombia?
The answer depends on the definition: what do we mean when we say, “level of education”? The definition should be consistent with the theory that motivates the hypothesis. Why should we expect a country’s level of education to affect whether it is democratic? What is it about education that we expect to translate into democratization?
As discussed in the preparatory video, some possible definitions and measurements for the level of education are the following:







Definition
Measurement




Accessibility of basic education to citizens.
Literacy rate


Proficiency of students in math, reading, and science.
Mean PISA score



Moreover, different approaches to measurement may generate variables of different types. Let’s review the types of variables:








Type of Variable
Definition
Examples




Nominal
Values are categories that cannot be ranked.
Political party, place of birth, election winner.


Ordinal
Values are categories that can be ranked.
Highest degree achieved, letter grade, military rank.


Interval
Values are numeric quantities that let us calculate the differences between them. Does not have a true zero.
Year of birth, body temperature, credit score.


Ratio
Values are numeric quantities that let us calculate the differences between them. Has a true zero.
Unemployment rate, annual income, percentage of votes for a candidate.

title: Activity: Proposing Measurement Strategies
text:
Proposing Measurement Strategies
Within your group, analyse each of the following hypotheses:

Ruthless dictators are more likely to stay in power for longer.
In religious countries, women participate less in politics than in secular countries.
States with oil reserves are less likely to have strict environmental regulations than states without oil reserves.

For each hypothesis:

Propose ways to measure each variable (dependent and independent).
Identify what type of variable your measurement strategy would generate.

title: Activity: Proposing Measurement Strategies
text:
Summary
In this activity, you have:

Practised moving from abstract concepts to concrete measurement strategies.
Identified the type of variable (nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio) that each measurement strategy produces.
Recognised that the same concept can be measured in different ways, and that the choice of measurement affects the type of variable and the analysis that follows.

text:

Producing and interpreting cross-tabulations, bar charts of means, and scatterplots with regression lines in Stata.

title: Activity: Country-level Correlations
text:
Introduction
This seminar has two parts. In the first hour, you will work through a set of variable pairs conceptually — identifying variable types, deciding which analytical case applies, and choosing the appropriate tool — without touching Stata. In the second hour, you will implement your choices in Stata and interpret the output.
Work through each part in order. Discuss your answers with your group before moving on.
The dataset for all exercises is the Quality of Government (QoG) dataset (available in our Shared Project Folder). Refer to the QoG codebook if you need more detail about any variable.

title: Activity: Country-level Correlations
text:
The Seven Variable Pairs
Below are seven pairs of variables drawn from the QoG dataset. Each pair is accompanied by a brief description of how each variable is measured and a research question that motivates the analysis. Read through all seven pairs before beginning Hour 1.

Pair 1
Variables: gol_est and ideavt_legvt

gol_est — Electoral system type (Bormann and Golder). Values: 1 = Majoritarian, 2 = Proportional, 3 = Mixed.
ideavt_legvt — Parliamentary election voter turnout (Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance). The percentage of the voting-age population that cast a vote in the most recent parliamentary election (0–100).

Research question: Do countries with different electoral systems differ in their average levels of voter turnout?


Pair 2
Variables: wdi_gini and ti_cpi

wdi_gini — Gini index (World Bank). A variable measuring income inequality within a country, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 100 (perfect inequality).
ti_cpi — Corruption Perceptions Index (Transparency International). A continuous variable ranging from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (highly clean), measuring perceptions of public sector corruption as seen by business people, risk analysts, and the general public.

Research question: Do more unequal countries tend to have higher levels of perceived corruption?


Pair 3
Variables: bmr_dem and ht_colonial

bmr_dem — Dichotomous democracy measure (Boix, Miller, and Rosato). This is a binary variable: 0 = not a democracy, 1 = democracy. Countries are coded as democratic if political leaders are chosen through free and fair elections and a minimum suffrage threshold is met. It does not measure degree of democracy.
ht_colonial — Colonial origin. A categorical variable recording the country’s former Western overseas colonial ruler (e.g. British, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Belgian). Countries that were never colonised by a Western overseas power are in a separate category.

Research question: Do countries with different colonial histories differ in their likelihood of being democratic today?


Pair 4
Variables: wdi_internet and rsf_pfi

wdi_internet — Individuals using the internet (World Bank). The percentage of the population with internet access (0–100).
rsf_pfi — Press Freedom Index (Reporters Without Borders). A numeric variable measuring the degree of freedom available to journalists and media organisations in each country. Higher scores indicate more press freedom.

Research question: Do countries with higher internet usage tend to have greater press freedom?


Pair 5
Variables: ht_colonial and ti_cpi

ht_colonial — Colonial origin. See Pair 3 for the full description.
ti_cpi — Corruption Perceptions Index. See Pair 2 for the full description.

Research question: Do countries with different colonial histories differ in their average levels of perceived corruption today?


Pair 6
Variables: gol_est and ht_region

gol_est — Electoral system type. See Pair 1 for the full description.
ht_region — Region of the world. A variable classifying countries into ten politico-geographic regions, including Eastern Europe and post-Soviet Union, Latin America, North Africa and the Middle East, Sub-Saharan Africa, Western Europe and North America, East Asia, South-East Asia, South Asia, the Pacific, and the Caribbean.

Research question: Do countries in different world regions tend to use different electoral systems?


Pair 7
Variables: wdi_gini and wdi_wip

wdi_gini — Gini index. See Pair 2 for the full description.
wdi_wip — Proportion of seats held by women in national parliaments (World Bank). Measured as a percentage (0–100).

Research question: Do more unequal countries tend to have lower levels of women’s representation in parliament?

title: Activity: Country-level Correlations
text:
Hour 1: Conceptual Mapping
In this hour, you will work through the seven pairs conceptually. Do not open Stata. For each pair, answer the three questions below by discussing with your group and writing down your answers.
For each of the seven pairs, answer:
Question A: What type is each variable?
Decide whether each variable is nominal (unordered categories), ordinal (ordered categories), or numeric (interval or ratio). Pay close attention to how the variable is measured — a variable coded as numbers is not necessarily numeric. Refer to the descriptions above and the codebook if needed.
Question B: Which analytical case applies?
Based on the variable types, determine which case this pair belongs to:

Case 1: Both variables are nominal → cross-tabulation and bivariate bar chart
Case 2: One nominal, one numeric → compare means and bar chart of means
Case 3: Both numeric → scatterplot and regression line

Question C: What is the appropriate tool?
State the specific plot or table you would use.

Once your group has worked through all seven pairs, be ready to discuss your answers. Pay particular attention to any pairs where you were uncertain — these are worth discussing carefully before moving to Hour 2.

title: Activity: Country-level Correlations
text:
Hour 2: Stata Implementation
In this hour, you will implement the tools you identified in Hour 1 and interpret the output. Work through the pairs in order, using bivariate-lecture.do as a reference for command syntax. For each pair, there are two steps: execute and interpret.

Pair 1 — gol_est and ideavt_legvt
Execute: Produce the appropriate summary table and chart.
Interpret:

Which electoral system is associated with the highest average turnout? Which with the lowest?
Is the difference between systems substantively meaningful, or are the means fairly similar?
Why might the choice of electoral system be associated with turnout? Think about how different systems create incentives for parties to mobilise voters.


Hint: A difference of a few percentage points in turnout can be politically significant at the national level, even if it looks modest in a chart.



Pair 2 — wdi_gini and ti_cpi
Execute: Produce the appropriate chart, including a regression line.
Interpret:

What is the direction of the association? Does a higher Gini index tend to be associated with higher or lower corruption scores?
Before interpreting the slope, make sure you have the scale direction of ti_cpi clearly in mind: a higher score means less corruption, not more. What does this imply about the slope you expect to see?


Hint: Getting the scale direction of ti_cpi right is essential for interpreting the slope correctly. Confirm which end of the scale represents more corruption before drawing conclusions.



Pair 3 — bmr_dem and ht_colonial
Execute: Produce the appropriate table and chart. When producing the table, try running it with both row percentages and column percentages.
Interpret:

Compare the row percentage output and the column percentage output. What does each tell you? Which is more useful for answering the research question, and why?
Are some colonial origins more strongly associated with democratic status than others? Which patterns stand out?


Hint: Row percentages show the distribution of one variable within each category of the other. Switching between row and column orientations reveals different aspects of the same association — think carefully about which question each answers.



Pair 4 — wdi_internet and rsf_pfi
Execute: Produce the appropriate chart, including a regression line.
Interpret:

Is there a positive association, a negative association, or no clear pattern?
Remember that higher rsf_pfi scores indicate more press freedom. If the slope is positive, what does that mean substantively?


Hint: Make sure you have the direction of the rsf_pfi scale clear before interpreting the slope. A positive slope here has a specific substantive meaning that depends on understanding what higher values represent.



Pair 5 — ht_colonial and ti_cpi
Execute: Produce the appropriate summary table and chart.
Interpret:

Which colonial-origin groups have the highest and lowest average corruption scores? Are the differences large or small?
Are there any groups represented by very few countries? How might this affect the reliability of the group mean?
Compare your findings here with Pair 2, which also involves ti_cpi. Both pairs ask about correlates of corruption, but use a different variable as the grouping factor. What does the comparison suggest about the sources of variation in corruption perceptions?


Hint: The bar chart of means lets you compare average corruption scores across colonial-origin categories at a glance. Look for categories with notably higher or lower means, and keep in mind that fewer countries in a category makes the average less reliable.



Pair 6 — gol_est and ht_region
Execute: Produce the appropriate table and chart.
Interpret:

Does electoral system type appear to be evenly distributed across regions, or does it cluster? Are there regions where one system type clearly dominates?
Are there any regions where data are sparse or missing? What might this imply?
Why might the choice of electoral system vary across world regions? Think about historical legacies, colonial influences, and the regional diffusion of institutional models.


Hint: A bivariate chart will make regional patterns easier to see than a table alone. Look for categories that are heavily concentrated in one region or largely absent from another.



Pair 7 — wdi_gini and wdi_wip
Execute: Produce the appropriate chart, including a regression line.
Interpret:

What does the slope of the regression line tell you about the direction of the relationship? Is a higher Gini index associated with more or fewer women in parliament?
Is the relationship strong or weak? How are the points distributed around the regression line?
Compare this with Pair 2, which also uses wdi_gini. Both pair inequality with a political outcome. Are the patterns similar or different? What might this suggest?


Hint: Pay attention to both the direction of the regression line and how tightly the points cluster around it. A flat or nearly flat line suggests little association, even if the slope is not exactly zero.

title: Activity: Country-level Correlations
text:
Summary
In this activity, you have:

Identified variable types and matched them to the appropriate bivariate analytical tool.
Produced and interpreted cross-tabulations, bar charts of means, and scatterplots with regression lines.
Connected descriptive patterns in data to theoretical arguments in political science.

These skills form the foundation for the independent empirical analysis you will carry out in Problem Set 2.

title: Activity: Sampling and Bias
text:
Introduction
A sample is biased if the units selected differ systematically from the population the researcher wants to study. Bias can arise from a flawed sampling frame, from non-random selection, from nonresponse, or from other features of the study design. In this activity you will examine five sampling scenarios and practise diagnosing these problems — the same reasoning the exam requires.
For each scenario, work through the three questions below with your group before moving on. Write down your answers: the exam will ask you to justify your reasoning in writing.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Sampling and Bias
text:
The Five Scenarios

Scenario A
A policy analyst working for a business association wants to know whether UK small businesses plan to transition to electric vehicle fleets over the next five years. The analyst obtains a list of all businesses currently registered with the Good Business Charter — a voluntary certification scheme for companies that commit to responsible environmental and employment practices. From this list, the analyst randomly selects 600 businesses and sends each a short online survey.
Questions:
A1. What is the population of interest in this study? Be precise: what group is the analyst trying to draw conclusions about?
A2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer. Your justification should show that you understand what distinguishes probability from non-probability sampling — not just which label applies.
A3. Would you expect this procedure to produce a biased or unbiased estimate of UK small businesses’ intentions to transition to electric fleets? If biased, would it overestimate or underestimate the proportion planning to transition? Justify your answer.



Scenario B
A King’s College London student believes that university accommodation in London is unaffordably expensive and wants to gather evidence to make the case to the Students’ Union. The student compiles a list of all KCL student halls of residence, randomly selects three halls, and over three separate days sets up a table near the entrance of each hall and asks students entering and leaving what they think about the cost of student accommodation in London.
Questions:
B1. What is the population of interest in this study?
B2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer.
B3. Would you expect this procedure to produce a biased or unbiased estimate of KCL student opinion on accommodation costs? If biased, in which direction? Justify your answer.



Scenario C
A researcher is commissioned by an environmental think tank to assess whether English local councils have been implementing policies to reduce carbon emissions. The researcher obtains a list of all 317 principal councils in England and emails the leader of a randomly selected sample of 200 councils, inviting them to complete a 10-minute survey about their council’s environmental policies over the past five years.
Questions:
C1. What is the population of interest in this study?
C2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer.
C3. Would you expect this procedure to produce a biased or unbiased estimate of the extent to which English councils have implemented environmental policies? If biased, in which direction? Justify your answer.



Scenario D
A criminologist wants to study the relationship between the provision of youth services and rates of anti-social behaviour across London boroughs. The researcher first categorises the 33 London boroughs into three groups based on how much they spend per capita on youth services: low, medium, and high. From each group, the researcher randomly selects four boroughs and conducts an in-depth study in those twelve boroughs.
Questions:
D1. What is the population of interest in this study?
D2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer.
D3. Are there any features of this design that might limit the conclusions the researcher can draw? Consider both the sampling procedure and the size of the sample relative to the population.



Scenario E
A market research company is hired by a major UK supermarket chain to measure customer satisfaction. The company randomly selects 30 stores from across the chain’s 600 locations. Staff at each selected store are asked to hand out short paper surveys to customers who are shopping at the time. Customers who agree to participate fill out the survey before leaving the store.
Questions:
E1. What is the population of interest in this study?
E2. Is this a probability sample or a non-probability sample? Justify your answer.
E3. Would you expect this procedure to produce a biased or unbiased estimate of customer satisfaction? If biased, in which direction? Justify your answer.
crumbs: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference

title: Activity: Sampling and Bias
text:
Synthesis
Once your group has worked through all five scenarios, discuss the following:
S1. Looking across all five scenarios: in which cases was random selection used somewhere in the design? Does the presence of random selection at one stage guarantee that the overall sample is unbiased? Why or why not?
S2. For the scenarios where you predicted bias, were the estimates more likely to overestimate or underestimate the quantity of interest? Is there a common pattern in what drives the direction of bias?
S3. The exam will present a single scenario and ask you to identify the population, classify the sampling procedure, and predict the direction of bias. Based on this activity, what are the key questions to ask yourself when working through a scenario like this?

title: Activity: Sampling and Bias

Diagnosed sources of bias in sampling procedures and predicted the direction of expected bias.

These are the core skills tested in Part Two of the exam.

title: Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Introduction
In Week 5, you described bivariate relationships between pairs of variables from the Quality of Government (QoG) dataset. For numeric–numeric pairs, you produced scatterplots with regression lines and described the direction and strength of the association visually.
This activity revisits three of those pairs. This time, you will move from description to inference: fitting a regression model, reading the output, and assessing statistical significance.
Work through each pair in order using regression-qog.do. The dataset is the Quality of Government (QoG) dataset (available in our Shared Project Folder). Refer to the QoG codebook if you need more detail about any variable.

title: Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Pair 1 — wdi_gini and wdi_wip
Variables:

wdi_gini — Gini index (World Bank). Measures income inequality within a country, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 100 (perfect inequality).
wdi_wip — Proportion of seats held by women in national parliaments (World Bank). Measured as a percentage (0–100).

Research question: Do more unequal countries tend to have lower levels of women’s representation in parliament?
Execute: Produce the scatterplot with regression line and run the regression.
Interpret:

What is the estimated slope for wdi_gini? Write out the full regression equation.
How do you interpret the slope substantively? For each one-unit increase in the Gini index, what change in women’s representation does the model predict?
Is the coefficient on wdi_gini statistically significant at the 5% level? How do you know?
What does the 95% confidence interval for the slope tell you?
What is the R-squared? What percentage of the variation in women’s parliamentary representation is explained by inequality?
Would you describe this as a strong, moderate, or weak relationship? What is your basis for that judgment?


Hint: Check the sign of the slope carefully. A negative slope would mean that higher inequality is associated with fewer women in parliament; a positive slope would mean the opposite. Make sure your substantive interpretation matches the sign.

title: Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Pair 2 — wdi_gini and ti_cpi
Variables:

wdi_gini — Gini index (World Bank). See Pair 1 for the full description.
ti_cpi — Corruption Perceptions Index (Transparency International). Ranges from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (highly clean). Higher scores indicate less corruption.

Research question: Do more unequal countries tend to have higher levels of perceived corruption?
Execute: Produce the scatterplot with regression line and run the regression.
Interpret:

What is the estimated slope for wdi_gini? Write out the full regression equation.
How do you interpret the slope substantively? For each one-unit increase in the Gini index, what change in the CPI does the model predict?
Is the coefficient on wdi_gini statistically significant at the 5% level? How do you know?
What does the 95% confidence interval for the slope tell you?
What is the R-squared? What percentage of the variation in corruption perceptions is explained by inequality?
Would you describe this as a strong, moderate, or weak relationship?


Hint: The CPI scale runs in the direction where higher = cleaner. A negative slope would mean that more unequal countries tend to score lower on the CPI — i.e., are perceived as more corrupt. Make sure your substantive interpretation accounts for the scale direction before drawing conclusions.

title: Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Pair 3 — wdi_internet and rsf_pfi
Variables:

wdi_internet — Individuals using the internet (World Bank). The percentage of the population with internet access (0–100).
rsf_pfi — Press Freedom Index (Reporters Without Borders). Measures the degree of freedom available to journalists and media organisations. Higher scores indicate more press freedom.

Research question: Do countries with higher internet usage tend to have greater press freedom?
Execute: Produce the scatterplot with regression line and run the regression.
Interpret:

What is the estimated slope for wdi_internet? Write out the full regression equation.
How do you interpret the slope substantively? For each one percentage point increase in internet usage, what change in press freedom does the model predict?
Is the coefficient on wdi_internet statistically significant at the 5% level? How do you know?
What does the 95% confidence interval for the slope tell you?
What is the R-squared? What percentage of the variation in press freedom is explained by internet usage?
Would you describe this as a strong, moderate, or weak relationship?


Hint: Remember that higher rsf_pfi scores mean more press freedom. A positive slope means that countries with more internet users tend to have greater press freedom. Think about why this relationship might exist — and whether you find it plausible.

title: Activity: Bivariate Regression
text:
Comparing the Three Models
Once you have worked through all three pairs, discuss the following questions with your group:

Which of the three relationships has the largest R-squared? What does this mean in terms of explanatory power?
Which relationship is most precisely estimated (i.e., has the narrowest confidence interval)? Does this correspond to the largest or smallest standard error?
All three slopes are estimated with uncertainty. For which pair, if any, would you be most cautious about drawing a strong substantive conclusion? Why?

title: Activity: Confounding and Reverse Causality
text:
Introduction
The concept videos for this week introduced two reasons why a correlation between X and Y may not reflect a causal relationship from X to Y.
Confounding variables. A confounding variable Z affects both X and Y but is not caused by X. It creates a spurious correlation: X and Y move together not because one causes the other, but because both are driven by Z. In the videos, we used the positive correlation between healthcare spending per capita and CO₂ emissions as an example: national wealth drives both, so the correlation does not imply that healthcare spending causes emissions.
We use three criteria to identify a confounding variable. Z is a confounder if it:

Affects the dependent variable (Y).
Affects the independent variable (X).
Is not a result of the independent variable (X).

Reverse causality. Reverse causality occurs when the assumed causal direction may be wrong. Even if X and Y are genuinely causally related, the data cannot tell us whether X causes Y, whether Y causes X, or whether causation runs in both directions. In the videos, we noted that higher CO₂ emissions may generate more pollution-related illness, increasing demand for healthcare — the opposite direction from what the original hypothesis assumed.
In this activity, you will apply both concepts to six new hypotheses. For each, work through the three questions with your group before moving on.
crumbs: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality

title: Activity: Confounding and Reverse Causality
text:
The Six Hypotheses

Hypothesis A
People with a library membership are more likely to get vaccinated.
A1. What is the independent variable (X) and the dependent variable (Y)?
A2. Identify one or more potential confounding variables. For each, explain how it satisfies the three criteria: (a) it affects vaccination uptake; (b) it affects library membership; (c) it is not caused by library membership.
A3. Is there a plausible reverse causal story? If so, describe it: explain how vaccination behaviour might cause library membership, or how the two might influence each other.



Hypothesis B
Famines are less likely in countries where there is press freedom.
B1. What is the independent variable (X) and the dependent variable (Y)?
B2. Identify one or more potential confounding variables. For each, explain how it satisfies the three criteria.
B3. Is there a plausible reverse causal story? If so, describe it.



Hypothesis C
Countries with fewer women in the national legislature tend to have more restrictive abortion policies.
C1. What is the independent variable (X) and the dependent variable (Y)?
C2. Identify one or more potential confounding variables. For each, explain how it satisfies the three criteria.
C3. Is there a plausible reverse causal story? If so, describe it.



Hypothesis D
Companies whose employees are more satisfied report higher profits.
D1. What is the independent variable (X) and the dependent variable (Y)?
D2. Identify one or more potential confounding variables. For each, explain how it satisfies the three criteria.
D3. Is there a plausible reverse causal story? If so, describe it.



Hypothesis E
Firms with higher levels of employee turnover have lower productivity.
E1. What is the independent variable (X) and the dependent variable (Y)?
E2. Identify one or more potential confounding variables. For each, explain how it satisfies the three criteria.
E3. Is there a plausible reverse causal story? If so, describe it.



Hypothesis F
Children who spend more time using electronic devices at a young age develop worse social skills.
F1. What is the independent variable (X) and the dependent variable (Y)?
F2. Identify one or more potential confounding variables. For each, explain how it satisfies the three criteria.
F3. Is there a plausible reverse causal story? If so, describe it.

title: Activity: Confounding and Reverse Causality
text:
Synthesis
Once your group has worked through all six hypotheses, discuss the following:
S1. For which hypothesis was reverse causality hardest to rule out? What made it difficult — was it that both causal directions were equally plausible, or that the data could not distinguish between them?
S2. For which hypothesis was a confounding variable easiest to identify? Was it the same hypothesis where reverse causality was most obvious, or a different one? What does this suggest about the relationship between the two threats to causal inference?
S3. In the exam, you may be asked to reason about a causal claim — identify threats to its validity and explain them clearly. Based on this activity, what are the key questions you should ask yourself when evaluating whether a correlation reflects a causal relationship?

title: Activity: Reading Regression Tables

Introduction
In Week 8, you ran bivariate regressions on Quality of Government (QoG) variables and interpreted the raw Stata output. In research papers and exams, regression results are presented in a more compact format: a regression table showing multiple models side by side. This activity practises reading that format.
The table below reports three regression models using the QoG dataset. The variables are:
Dependent variable:

Press Freedom Index (rsf_pfi): measurement of press freedom for each country according to Reporters Without Borders. Higher scores indicate more press freedom.

Independent variables:

Internet Users (%) (wdi_internet): percentage of the population with internet access. Source: World Development Indicators.
Gini Index (wdi_gini): a measure of income inequality within a country, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 100 (perfect inequality). Source: World Development Indicators.

The researchers pose two research questions:

Do countries with higher internet usage tend to have greater press freedom?
Do more unequal countries tend to have less press freedom?

title: Activity: Reading Regression Tables
text:
Questions
Work through the following questions in your group. Refer to Table 1 for all answers.
Q1. According to Model 1, what is the estimated slope for internet users? What is its standard error?
Q2. According to Model 1, for each one percentage point increase in internet users, what is the predicted change in the Press Freedom Index? Is this change positive or negative, and what does it mean substantively?
Q3. According to Model 2, what would be the predicted Press Freedom Index of a hypothetical country with a Gini index of zero (i.e., perfect equality)? Which number in the table gives you this prediction?
Q4. Is the coefficient on the Gini index statistically significant at the 5% level in Model 2? What about in Model 3? How can you tell from the table?

Hint: Look at the stars next to each coefficient. The note at the bottom of the table tells you what each star level means. Remember that a coefficient is significant at the 5% level if its p-value is less than 0.05.

Q5. Using Model 3, calculate the predicted Press Freedom Index for a country where 70% of the population uses the internet and the Gini index is 40. Show your calculation.

Hint: Write out the regression equation using the constant and the two slope coefficients from Model 3, then substitute the values.

Q6. Compare the coefficient on the Gini index between Models 2 and 3. In which model is the coefficient larger in magnitude? Why do you think the coefficient changes when internet usage is added to the model?
Q7. Which model has the highest R²? Does adding inequality to the internet model (comparing Models 1 and 3) substantially increase the proportion of variation explained?
Q8. Can you think of a variable not included in these models that could be a confounding variable for the relationship between internet usage and press freedom? Explain how it meets the definition of a confounding variable: it must plausibly affect both the independent variable and the dependent variable.

Hint: Think about what characteristics of a country might simultaneously affect how many people use the internet and how free the press is.

title: CLAUDE.md — Rules for the attention-checks/ directory
text:
CLAUDE.md — Rules for the attention-checks/ directory
This file defines rules specific to the attention-checks directory.
These rules supplement the repository-wide rules defined in the root CLAUDE.md.
Claude must follow both.



Purpose
Attention checks are short quiz questions embedded in the H5P interactive videos on KEATS (Moodle).
Each video should have at least one attention check. The questions appear during playback to verify that students are engaging with the material.



File Naming Convention
Files use the same prefix and slug as the corresponding slide page:
{prefix}{nn}-{topic-slug}.txt
Where the prefix matches the slide family:

C for concept videos (matching slides/videos-concepts/)
S for Stata videos (matching slides/videos-stata/)

Examples:

C01-empirical-vs-normative.txt corresponds to slides/videos-concepts/C01-empirical-vs-normative.qmd
S01-doing-reproducible-research.txt corresponds to slides/videos-stata/S01-doing-reproducible-research.qmd




File Format
Attention check files are plain .txt files with a simple structure.
Each file contains one or more questions. Each question consists of:

A question stem (one or more lines of text)
A blank line
Answer options, each on its own line, prefixed with -
The first option listed is always the correct answer

Questions within the same file are separated by a blank line after the last option of the preceding question.
Example:
What is reproducible research?

- Being able to obtain the same results using the same data and code
- Being able to prove that your hypothesis is correct
- Being able to formulate a good theory for a research question



Question Design Conventions

Questions are short and test a single concept from the video.
Most questions have three options; some have four. Two options is the minimum.
The correct answer is always listed first in the file. H5P shuffles the options when displaying them to students.
Distractors should be plausible but clearly wrong to a student who watched the video.
Some questions include a quoted scenario or hypothesis before the question stem.
The tone is informal and accessible. Occasional humour in distractors is acceptable.
A file may contain one question or several, depending on the length of the video.




Coverage
Attention checks exist for:

All 28 concept videos (C01–C28)
Stata videos S01–S04, S09–S11

Stata videos S05–S08 do not yet have attention checks.
There are no attention checks for lecture slides (the W-series), since lectures are not delivered as H5P interactive videos.
Claude must not create attention checks for missing videos unless explicitly instructed.



Allowed Tasks in attention-checks/
Claude may:

Create new attention check files when instructed
Add questions to existing files
Improve question clarity
Fix formatting issues

Claude must not:

Change the file format (plain .txt, first option = correct answer)
Rename or move existing files
Create attention checks for videos that do not exist

title: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Introduction
In research, it can be tempting to jump straight to “testing something” without being clear about what you are asking, what explanation you find plausible, and what you would expect to observe if that explanation were correct.
This activity gives you a simple workflow that you will use repeatedly in this module:
research question → theory → hypothesis

title: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Overview

Descriptive questions ask what the world looks like. They describe distributions, trends, or correlations.
Causal questions ask what would happen if we intervened. They ask whether changing one thing would change another.
A theory is a reasoned and precise speculation about the answer to a research question.
A hypothesis is an empirically testable implication of a theory: given your theory, what should we observe in the world?

title: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Examples

Descriptive vs causal
Descriptive questions:

What percentage of countries are democratic?
Is there a global trend towards democratic backsliding?
Is democratic backsliding more prevalent in countries with higher political polarisation?

Causal questions:

Does exposure to divisive content on social media make people more tolerant of political violence?
Does declining trust in political elites weaken commitment to democratic norms?
Do compulsory voting laws increase political participation?



From theory to hypothesis

Research question: How did countries’ health care systems affect their abilities to mitigate the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic?
Theory: Countries with public health care systems took advantage of their centralised bureaucracies to implement more effective policy responses.
Hypothesis: Countries with public health care systems had lower Covid death rates than countries with private health care systems.

title: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Tasks
Work in groups of about three. Your goal is to produce one coherent chain consisting of a research question, a classification (descriptive/causal), one theory, and one hypothesis.

1. Formulate a research question

Write one empirical research question about a social or political phenomenon.
Your question should be answerable in principle with data (even if you do not yet know what data you would use).



2. Classify your question

Is your question descriptive or causal? Write one sentence explaining why.



3. State one theory

Write one theory: a reasoned and precise speculation about the answer to your research question.
The theory should explain why (not just restate the question).



4. Derive one hypothesis

Write one hypothesis implied by your theory.
The hypothesis should be empirically testable and should make clear what you would expect to observe in the world.

title: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
text:
Quick self-check

Does the theory address the research question directly?

Does the hypothesis follow logically from the theory?

If the hypothesis were false, would that count against the theory (at least as stated)?

title: Proposing Measurement Strategies
text:
Introduction
Hypothesis: Countries with higher levels of education are more likely to be democratic than countries with lower levels of education.
How should we measure the level of education? What information should we rely on to determine whether Mexico is more or less educated than Colombia?
The answer depends on the definition: what do we mean when we say, “level of education”? The definition should be consistent with the theory that motivates the hypothesis. Why should we expect a country’s level of education to affect whether it is democratic? What is it about education that we expect to translate into democratization?
As discussed in the preparatory video, some possible definitions and measurements for the level of education are the following:







Definition
Measurement




Accessibility of basic education to citizens.
Literacy rate


Proficiency of students in math, reading, and science.
Mean PISA score



Moreover, different approaches to measurement may generate variables of different types. Let’s review the types of variables:








Type of Variable
Definition
Examples




Nominal
Values are categories that cannot be ranked.
Political party, place of birth, election winner.


Ordinal
Values are categories that can be ranked.
Highest degree achieved, letter grade, military rank.


Interval
Values are numeric quantities that let us calculate the differences between them. Does not have a true zero.
Year of birth, body temperature, credit score.


Ratio
Values are numeric quantities that let us calculate the differences between them. Has a true zero.
Unemployment rate, annual income, percentage of votes for a candidate.

title: Proposing Measurement Strategies
text:
Proposing measurement strategies
Within your group, analyze each of the following hypotheses:

Ruthless dictators are more likely to stay in power for longer.
In religious countries, women participate less in politics than in secular countries.
States with oil reserves are less likely to have strict environmental regulations than states without oil reserves.

For each hypothesis:

Propose ways to measure each variable (dependent and independent).
Identify what type of variable your measurement strategy would generate.

title: Handoff: Week 11 Dummy Variables Lecture — 2026-03-29
text:
Three files were created for the final lecture of the course (Week 11: Dummy Variables):

slides/lectures/W11-dummy-variables.qmd — 27-slide lecture deck
shared-project-folder/do/dummy-bes.do — student-facing Stata do-file
_quarto.yml — modified to add Week 11 sidebar section




This lecture introduces dummy variables as independent variables while integrating a critical discussion about interpreting coefficients on immutable characteristics as causal effects. The critical discussion happens during the lecture itself (no separate seminar activity; the Week 11 seminar is fully dedicated to PS2 Workshop 4).



Technical intro (slides 1-7): What dummies are, coding, reference categories, interpretation of B0 and B1. Kept brisk because students already understand regression mechanics from Weeks 8-10.
Gender-ideology regression (slides 8-13): Regress left-right ideology (e01, 0-10 scale) on a woman dummy using BES 2024 data with survey weights. Students run the do-file and interpret the output. Then: “Can we call this causal?”
Counterfactual criterion (slides 14-21): This is the new conceptual contribution. Students already know about confounders (Week 9) and reverse causality (Week 9). This lecture adds a third lens: even absent confounders, causal language requires a meaningful counterfactual. For immutable characteristics like gender, the counterfactual (“what if this person were not a woman?”) is ill-defined.

The Zuberi/Bonilla-Silva quote is the nudging mechanism: “Empirical results may be a way to understand what is happening; however, these same data tell us very little about why it happens.” It is presented alongside the discussion question, not after a failed causal interpretation.
Students brainstorm social processes (socialisation, structural inequality) that produce the gender gap, reinforcing that the coefficient conflates many factors.
A corrective slide clarifies: dummies are useful tools; the coefficient describes real group differences; the problem is only in causal interpretation.

Pearson case and closing (slides 22-27): Karl Pearson (founder of modern statistics) published “The Problem of Alien Immigration” (1928) in the Annals of Eugenics, using correlations of physical measurements of Jewish immigrant children to argue that observed differences were innate racial traits, not environmental. His concluding paragraph is quoted on a slide. The policy relevance: this was explicitly framed as an argument for immigration restriction, lending statistical authority to prejudiced conclusions. The lecture closes with a course recap and the message: “Data literacy makes good citizens.”





Technical and critical content are integrated, not sequential
The gender example is the vehicle, not the destination
The Pearson case amplifies stakes without dominating
The lecture ends on an empowering note, not cautionary
Scope is limited to dummies as IVs (dummies as DVs deferred to Stats 2)
BES data used throughout, consistent with rest of course




The quote from Zuberi/Bonilla-Silva serves as the nudge. It is presented alongside the discussion question rather than after students attempt a causal interpretation. Rationale: students have been taught all term that correlation does not imply causation, so they are unlikely to naively assert causality. The pedagogical challenge is getting them to articulate why the causal interpretation fails in a new way (counterfactual, not just confounders).




svy: regress e01 woman     (N = 2,652)

         e01 | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
       woman |  -.3955786   .0853191    -4.64   0.000    -.5628773   -.2282799
       _cons |   4.981491   .0634301    78.54   0.000     4.857113    5.105868

Men’s mean ideology: 4.98 (intercept)
Women score 0.40 points lower (more left-leaning), p < 0.001
R-squared = 0.01 (gender explains 1% of variation)





Review the slide deck — read through slides/lectures/W11-dummy-variables.qmd and flag any slides where pacing, wording, or sequencing should change
Render the lecture — run quarto render slides/lectures/W11-dummy-variables.qmd to verify it compiles
Optionally render the full site — if satisfied, run quarto render to rebuild everything (this also verifies the sidebar)





Legacy UCSD slides: legacy/slides/L14_Dummy.pdf (technical structure for dummy variable cases)
Legacy UCSD activity: legacy/activities/CA19_Critical.docx (Zuberi/Bonilla-Silva quote, POC regression activity)
Pearson & Moul (1928): documents/Pearson_Moul_1928.pdf (historical case; concluding paragraph on p. 264)
Pattern files: hypothesis-bes.do (BES data cleaning, svyset), W10-multivariate.qmd (lecture structure)
