title: Handoff: Mock Exam and Activity Harmonisation — 2026-04-01
text:
Activities from earlier in the module that were previously distributed as Word/Rmd documents were converted to .qmd and published on the website:

activities/A01-quant-qual.qmd — Week 1: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research (from documents/L01-quant-qual.docx)
activities/A02-questions-theories-hypotheses.qmd — Week 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses (from documents/L02-questions-theories-hypotheses.Rmd)
activities/A03-propose-measurement.qmd — Week 3: Proposing Measurement Strategies (from documents/S03-propose-measurement.Rmd)

All three were added to _quarto.yml under their respective week sections.



All activity files in activities/ were updated with three changes:

Titles now use the Activity: prefix (replacing “Mock Exam Question:”, “Seminar Activity:”, “Group Activity:”, “Catch-Up Activity:”, “PS2 Workshop N:”)
Horizontal rules removed from all files
“What you’ll practice” section added as the first section in every activity (A01-A03 already had one; A04-A11 received new ones)

reference/activities_metadata.csv was updated to reflect all new titles.



documents/4SSPP111_Mock_Exam.docx — a full-length practice exam (100 points, 13 questions, 3 parts) formatted to match the actual exam papers.
Structure:

Part 1: Descriptive Analysis (25 pts, Q1-Q5) — NSS student satisfaction histogram. Broader than the actual exams: includes variable type (Q1), histogram reading (Q2), skewness identification (Q3), mean vs median reasoning (Q4), and descriptive vs causal claim (Q5). The extra topics signal to students that these are fair game.
Part 2: Sampling (25 pts, Q6-Q8) — Councillor at a leisure centre scenario. Population of interest, probability vs non-probability, bias direction.
Part 3: Regression (50 pts, Q9-Q13) — Brexit regression table (Higher Education + Immigrant Share predicting Leave Vote Share). Slope interpretation, predicted value from intercept, predicted value from multivariate model, significance comparison (Immigrant Share loses significance in Model 3), confounding variable.

Supporting files:

documents/4SSPP111_Mock_Exam.qmd — source file used to generate the .docx via pandoc
r/mock_exam_reg_table.R — R script that generates the stargazer HTML table
documents/mock_exam_reg_table.html — stargazer output, copy-pasted into the Word document manually

The regression table in the .docx was finalised by the user after copy-pasting the stargazer HTML output and making manual formatting adjustments.







NSS histogram: Left-skewed, which enables a mean vs median question. Students have seen it in the concept video (C09) but not in either real exam.
Leisure centre scenario: Clear non-probability sampling with unambiguous bias direction (overestimates support for cycle lane because leisure centre users are more physically active).
Brexit regression table: From the concept video (C28). Students have studied it before. Features a variable that loses significance in the multivariate model (Immigrant Share), enabling a significance comparison question.





Reverse causality question — removed because the Brexit case makes reverse causality awkward (education → Leave voting is hard to reverse plausibly, which could confuse students rather than test their understanding).
Topics left out of the mock exam: quantitative vs qualitative reasoning (too open-ended), survey weights (too fine-grained for the exam), visual inference / CI overlap heuristic (hard to test without fabricating a plot), choosing bivariate tools (mechanical, tested in PS2).




Part 1 is 25 points (vs 15 in the actual exams) because it includes two extra question types (mean/median, descriptive/causal). Part 3 is 50 points (vs 60 in May) because the reverse causality question was removed.




A detailed mapping was produced during this session showing which conceptual activities and lecture activities map to which exam questions, and which topics are covered in activities but not tested. This mapping informed the mock exam design. The full mapping is in the conversation history but was not saved to a separate file.




Review the mock exam .docx — open the Word document and verify formatting, especially the regression table after the manual copy-paste.
Decide how to distribute — the mock exam could be shared via the Shared Project Folder (OneDrive), posted on KEATS, or linked from the website. This was not decided during the session.
Consider creating an answer key — the plan file at .claude/plans/spicy-stirring-pie.md contains expected answers for all 13 questions. These could be formatted into a separate document if needed.
Render the site — the three new activities and the harmonisation changes have not been rendered. A full quarto render is needed before publishing.

title: MEMORY.md — Methods Education Website
text:
This repository contains a Quarto website used to host teaching materials for a university module on research methods and statistics.
The site publishes lecture slides, concept explanations, activities, quizzes, and reference pages.
All materials are written in Quarto (.qmd) and rendered as a static website hosted on GitHub Pages.
The goal of the project is to provide students with structured teaching materials combining slide explanations and lecture videos.




The site uses HTML pages as the primary navigation format.
Each slide deck has two formats:

HTML page view (default navigation format)
RevealJS slide presentation

Students normally read the HTML page view.
RevealJS is available through the “Other Formats → RevealJS” link and is mainly used for presenting slides in class.




Most slide pages follow this structure:

YouTube lecture video embed (when available)
Structured headings explaining concepts
Optional link to the RevealJS slide format

Videos are embedded directly inside the .qmd page using the full YouTube embed code.
There is currently no reusable embed template.




Video integration is still in progress.

Some lecture videos have been uploaded to YouTube.
Only some of those videos are currently embedded on the site.
Many pages still do not contain embedded videos.

At a later stage the embedding process may be completed programmatically using Claude Code.




Content directories:
slides/ — lecture and concept slide decks
activities/ — interactive exercises
quizzes/ — quiz material attention-checks/ — classroom attention checks reference/ — project reference material
Shared resources:
assets/ — images and media cards/ — thumbnail images for YouTube video uploads theme/ — SCSS theme files controlling slide styling




reference/videos_metadata.csv
This file contains structured metadata about lecture videos.
It may be used to guide the creation or updating of slide pages.
The file is read-only for Claude unless explicitly instructed.




These directories are generated automatically by Quarto and must not be edited.
.quarto/
_freeze/
_site/




_quarto.yml — defines site navigation and rendering
styles.css — site-level styling
theme/ — RevealJS styling




The site uses a left sidebar navigation panel.
Sidebar items link to HTML page versions of slide decks and activities.
RevealJS slides are accessed through the “Other Formats” menu.




The site is rendered locally with Quarto and deployed to GitHub Pages.
Typical workflow:

edit .qmd files
preview locally with quarto preview
render the site
publish changes

Claude Code must never perform deployment actions.




shared-project-folder/ is a student-facing teaching resource shared via OneDrive (view-only for students). It is gitignored.
It contains:

data-raw/ — original datasets (.dta) and codebooks
data-clean/ — cleaned datasets produced by do-files
do/ — Stata do-files used in teaching
output/ — graphs generated by do-files

The do-files in this folder are the actual statistical code that the course teaching materials walk students through. Lecture slides, seminar activities, and problem sets on the website all reference analyses performed by these do-files with these datasets.
This tight coupling means that Claude Code’s ability to read, edit, and execute these do-files is central to maintaining and developing the course.




Claude Code can execute Stata do-files from the terminal and read the output.
This was established on 2026-03-15 after resolving three layered Windows compatibility issues (MSYS2 path mangling, GUI process control, and output capture).
The full invocation recipe is documented in CLAUDE.md under “Running Stata from Claude Code”.
High-level approach:

Write a wrapper do-file to C:\temp\ with log using / log close / exit, clear
Execute via MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 powershell -Command 'Start-Process ... -Wait'
Read C:\temp\stata-output.log for the output

Stata executable: C:\Program Files\Stata19\StataSE-64.exe




legacy/ contains UCSD-era teaching materials (slides, transcripts, reference pages, activities, planning prompts). These are gitignored and read-only.
New slide decks and videos for the KCL course are created using legacy materials as starting points. The process involves reading the legacy source, adapting the pedagogical structure, and replacing examples with UK datasets (Brexit, BES, QoG, NSS).
The UCSD materials used California county / Trump vote data as the running example. The KCL materials use Brexit Regional data (education, import shock, unemployment predicting Leave vote share) as the primary regression example.
See legacy/CLAUDE.md for the full file inventory and the mapping between legacy sources and current pages.

legacy/ contains UCSD-era teaching materials (slides, transcripts, reference pages, activities, planning prompts). These are gitignored and read-only.
New slide decks and videos for the KCL course are created using legacy materials as starting points. The process involves reading the legacy source, adapting the pedagogical structure, and replacing examples with UK datasets (Brexit, BES, QoG, NSS).
The UCSD materials used California county / Trump vote data as the running example. The KCL materials use Brexit Regional data (education, import shock, unemployment predicting Leave vote share) as the primary regression example.
See legacy/CLAUDE.md for the full file inventory and the mapping between legacy sources and current pages.

I’m resuming work on the Week 11 dummy variables lecture that was drafted in a previous session on another machine. Please read the handoff document at @logs/2026-03-29-handoff.md to understand the full pedagogical design and current state.
Then read the slide deck at @slides/lectures/W11-dummy-variables.qmd and the do-file at @shared-project-folder/do/dummy-bes.do.
I’d like to review the slides and make adjustments before rendering. I’ll tell you what I want to change after you’ve read everything.

title: Exam Review Guide
text: This page is a topic-by-topic guide for revising for the 4SSPP111 final exam. Topics are grouped by the resources that prepare you for them: each block lists what you should be able to do, then the videos, slides, and activity that cover the whole block.

title: Exam Review Guide
text:
Practical exam information

Duration: 2 hours.
Total marks: 100, across 12 questions in three parts.
Calculator: Casio Fx83 or Fx85 only.
Notes allowed: one sheet of A4 paper with handwritten notes on both sides.
No Stata commands are tested. The exam assesses reasoning and interpretation, not Stata syntax.
Answer all questions.

title: Exam Review Guide
text:
How to use this guide
For each topic block:

Watch the linked concept videos.
Review the corresponding lecture slides.
Redo the seminar activity from memory, then check your answers.

When you have worked through the blocks, attempt the Mock Exam (available on KEATS) under timed conditions, then compare your answers against the Mock Exam Answer Key (also on KEATS). The mock does not cover every possible exam topic, so do not treat it as an exhaustive list.

title: Exam Review Guide
text:
Part 1 — Descriptive analysis

Research questions, theories, and hypotheses

Distinguish empirical from normative questions.
Identify dependent and independent variables in a quantitative claim.
Recognise the role of theory and hypothesis in framing a quantitative claim.

Resources:

Concept video: Normative and Empirical Questions
Concept video: Units of Analysis, Theories, and Hypotheses
Concept video: Dependent and Independent Variables
Lecture: Week 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
Activity: Research Questions, Theories and Hypotheses



Measuring variables

Evaluate how a chosen measurement strategy shapes the conclusions a piece of research can support.

Resources:

Concept video: Measuring Variables
Lecture: Week 3: Measurement and Variable Types
Activity: Proposing Measurement Strategies



Variable types

Classify a variable as nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio.
Justify the classification by reference to its measurement properties (categories, ordering, equal intervals, true zero).

Resources:

Concept video: Types of Variables
Concept video: Measuring Variables
Lecture: Week 3: Measurement and Variable Types
Activity: Proposing Measurement Strategies



Distributions: histograms, shape, and central tendency

Read approximate counts from histogram bars and compare counts across ranges.
Identify whether a distribution is symmetric, left-skewed, or right-skewed.
Predict whether the mean is greater than, less than, or approximately equal to the median based on the shape of the distribution, and explain why.

Resources:

Concept video: Summarising a Distribution
Concept video: Variance and Standard Deviation
Concept video: Bar Charts and Histograms
Lab video: Bar Charts and Histograms in Stata
Lecture: Week 4: Describing Distributions
Activity: Describing Distributions



Descriptive vs causal claims

Identify whether a claim is descriptive or causal.
Explain the wording or reasoning that makes it one or the other.

Resources:

Concept video: Descriptive and Causal Questions
Lecture: Week 2: Research Questions, Theories, and Hypotheses
Activity: Research Questions, Theories and Hypotheses

title: Exam Review Guide
text:
Part 2 — Sampling, estimation, and uncertainty

Population, sampling, and bias

Identify the population of interest in a research scenario.
Classify a sampling procedure as probability or non-probability, and justify the classification by reference to whether every member of the population has a known, non-zero chance of selection.
Assess whether a sampling procedure is likely to produce a biased estimate, predict the direction of the bias, and explain the mechanism that produces it.

Resources:

Concept video: Why Sampling Matters
Lecture: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference
Activity: Sampling and Bias

title: Exam Review Guide
text:
Part 3 — Regression and causal inference

Bivariate regression: slope and intercept

State the predicted change in the dependent variable associated with a one-unit change in the independent variable, including units and direction.
State the predicted value of the dependent variable when the independent variable equals zero (the intercept).

Resources:

Concept video: Regression Analysis: Introduction
Concept video: Regression Slope
Lecture: Week 8: Regression Analysis
Activity: Bivariate Regression



Multivariate regression and predicted values

Read a multivariate regression table.
Compute a predicted value of the dependent variable given values for each independent variable, using the regression equation. Show your calculations.

Resources:

Concept video: Multivariate Regression: Adding Controls
Concept video: Reading Regression Tables for Publication
Lecture: Week 10: Multivariate Regression
Activity: Reading Regression Tables



Statistical significance

Read significance stars in a regression table and identify which coefficients are statistically significant.
Explain what non-significance means in terms of the null hypothesis.
Relate the size of a coefficient to its standard error.

Resources:

Concept video: Interpreting P-values
Concept video: Inference in Regression: CIs and P-values
Concept video: The Standard Error
Lecture: Week 7: Estimation, Uncertainty, and Statistical Inference
Lecture: Week 8: Regression Analysis
Lecture: Week 10: Multivariate Regression
Activity: Bivariate Regression



Confounding, reverse causality, and random assignment

Define a confounding variable, propose a plausible confounder for a given regression, and justify the proposal by explaining how the confounder relates to both the independent and dependent variables.
Assess whether a causal claim can plausibly be challenged on grounds of reverse causality, and explain the direction of the alternative causal pathway.
Explain how random assignment supports causal inference, and why observational regressions cannot, on their own, support the same kind of causal claim.

Resources:

Concept video: Confounding Variables
Concept video: Reverse Causality
Concept video: Random Assignment and Causal Inference
Concept video: Controls and Confounding in Multivariate Regression
Lecture: Week 9: Confounding Variables and Reverse Causality
Lecture: Week 10: Multivariate Regression
Activity: Confounding and Reverse Causality
Activity: Reading Regression Tables



Dummy variables and counterfactual reasoning

Interpret the intercept and slope of a regression that includes a dummy variable as the independent variable.
Assess whether a counterfactual implied by a regression specification is plausible, and explain why the plausibility of the counterfactual matters for the interpretation of an estimate.

Resources:

Lecture: Week 11: Dummy Variables

title: Exam Review Guide
text:
Final preparation
Once you have worked through the blocks above, attempt the Mock Exam (available on KEATS) under timed conditions: two hours, calculator, one A4 sheet of handwritten notes. After completing it, compare your answers against the Mock Exam Answer Key (also on KEATS). Use any gaps you find as a steer for further revision.

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Welcome

Please call me Leo
Today’s goals:

Clarify what this module is and is not
Explain how lectures, seminars, and assessments fit together
Set expectations for Problem Sets
Work through a group activity on quantitative vs qualitative research

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
What This Module Is About
This module is about:

Thinking clearly with data
Understanding what statistical claims can and cannot show
Evaluating evidence in political science research
Learning how to ask and test empirical questions

It is not about memorising formulas or becoming a statistician

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
section: Why the Module Is Structured This Way
text:
Why the Module Is Structured This Way
The module uses a flipped format:

Short videos and quizzes before lectures
Lectures and seminars focus on active learning
Problem Sets reinforce concepts gradually over time
This structure is based on evidence from education research

Eg, Ambrose et al 2007, Nilson 2010

How PS1 Works (Core Rules)

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Quizzes vs Videos (Important Distinction)

Quizzes

5–10 multiple-choice questions
Unlimited attempts
Highest score counts
Deadlines are enforced

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data

Quizzes vs Videos (Important Distinction)

Videos

Include attention-check questions
One attempt per question
Videos remain accessible throughout the term

If you miss a quiz, you can still earn partial credit for that week via the videos.

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Flexibility Built In

There are eight weeks with PS1 activities
Your best six weekly scores count
The two lowest scores are dropped
This is designed as insurance, not a target

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
section: Why We Focus on Quantitative Research
text:
Why We Focus on Quantitative Research
This module focuses on quantitative methods, but:

That does not mean qualitative research is inferior
Different methods answer different kinds of questions
Understanding the distinction helps you evaluate evidence critically

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
section: Group Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research
text:
Group Activity: Quantitative vs Qualitative Research

You will work in small groups
The goals are to:

Understand how quantitative and qualitative research differ
Reflect on what each approach does well
Discuss what each approach may miss

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Two Research Traditions (Mahoney & Goertz)
Quantitative research

Average effects across cases
General, law-like claims
Example: What is the effect of economic development on democracy?

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Two Research Traditions (Mahoney & Goertz)
Qualitative research

Specific outcomes in particular cases
Less emphasis on generalisation
Example: Did economic development contribute to Spain’s transition to democracy?

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Example: Studying Democratisation
Quantitative approach

Large dataset of countries
GDP per capita, democracy scores, controls
Statistical analysis of average relationships

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Example: Studying Democratisation
Qualitative approach

One or more case studies
Archives, interviews, historical evidence
Tracing causal processes within cases

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Your Task

Discuss advantages and disadvantages of each approach
Think about:

What does this approach allow us to see?
What does it obscure or miss?

Pros
Cons

title: Lecture 1: Thinking With Data
text:
Reconvening
We will reconvene and:

Collect examples from different groups
Compare perspectives
Discuss why mixed-method approaches are increasingly common

section: Why This Matters for the Module
text:
Why This Matters for the Module
Although this course focuses on quantitative methods:

You should always ask what a method can and cannot show
Statistical results are not self-interpreting
Good political science depends on methodological awareness

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
Welcome
Today’s goals:

Recap the core points from this week’s videos
Work through a group discussion on measuring democracy

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
Example: Education levels and democratisation

Research question: Do higher levels of education make countries more likely to democratise?

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
Level of education

How do we know if a country’s level of education is high or low?
What information do we collect?
We should start by figuring out a definition for the level of education.

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
Defining the level of education

Accessibility of basic education to all citizens?
Proficiency of students in reading, math, and science?
The implications for research are not trivial!

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
From definition to measurement

A measurement for accessibility: Literacy rates.

A good (but not perfect) approximation.

A measurement for proficiency: Students’ standardised exam scores.

PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment).

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text: Literacy rates

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text: PISA scores

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
From education to democracy

Research question: Is there a global trend towards democratic backsliding?
A pressing contemporary debate that highlights the importance of measurement choices.
Recent debates focus on a particular measurement: Varieties of Democracy (V-DEM).

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
Varieties of Democracy (V-DEM)

Democracy measured as an interval variable (countries are given scores between 0 and 1)
Sends questionnaires to over 3,700 country experts.
Questions about several indicators deemed necessary to determine if a country is democratic.

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
section: The critique: Little & Meng (2024) on V-Dem
text:
The critique: Little & Meng (2024) on V-Dem

V-Dem relies heavily on expert judgments, which may shift over time even if underlying political institutions do not.
Changes in expert expectations or standards can look like changes in democracy.
As an alternative, Little and Meng argue for focusing on indicators of democracy that are less sensitive to subjective interpretation.

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
section: What does their alternative look like?
text:
What does their alternative look like?
Little and Meng (2024) propose measuring democracy using indicators as:

Whether incumbents and ruling parties lose elections and accept defeat.
The degree of electoral competition, including vote shares and seat shares of winning parties.
The presence and enforcement of formal institutional constraints, such as term limits and succession rules.

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
The counter-critique: V-DEM’s side
Scholars associated with V-Dem respond that:

Democracy is inherently multidimensional and cannot be adequately captured by a narrow set of observable outcomes.
Indicators presented as “objective” by Little and Meng still involve coding decisions and theoretical assumptions; they are not free from subjectivity.
Expert-based measures are not a feature, not a bug for measuring complex political concepts.

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
section: Group activity: How to measure democracy?
text:
Group activity: How to measure democracy?

In small groups, discuss the debate you have just seen.
Your task is not to decide whether democracy is declining, but to decide which approach to measurement you find more convincing.
Focus on the trade-offs between expert judgment and more “objective” indicators, and on what each approach can and cannot capture.

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
Guiding questions for discussion

Which critique or defense do you find more persuasive, and why?
What do you think is lost when we move away from expert judgments?
What do you think is lost when we rely heavily on subjective assessments?
If you had to choose one approach to answer the question of democratic backsliding, which would you choose?

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:

Click here, scan the QR code, or join at menti.com using the code 2173 3787

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
Dig Deeper

How steep is Trump’s democratic backsliding?

Financial Times, 31 Jan 2026 (Access with your King’s email account).

Methodology reviewed by Anne Meng.

title: Lecture 3: Measurement and Types of Variables
text:
Why this matters

Measurement choices are not neutral. They shape what we see in the data and the conclusions we draw from it.
Different definitions and measurements of the same concept can lead to very different answers to the same research question.

Democracy is inherently multidimensional and cannot be adequately captured by a narrow set of observable outcomes.
Indicators presented as “objective” by Little and Meng still involve coding decisions and theoretical assumptions; they are not free from subjectivity.
Expert-based measures are not a feature, not a bug for measuring complex political concepts.

Group activity: How to measure democracy?

In small groups, discuss the debate you have just seen.
Your task is not to decide whether democracy is declining, but to decide which approach to measurement you find more convincing.
Focus on the trade-offs between expert judgment and more “objective” indicators, and on what each approach can and cannot capture.

If you had to choose one approach to answer the question of democratic backsliding, which would you choose?

section: Example: Education and the Leave vote
text:
Example: Education and the Leave vote

Research question: Do regions with higher education shares vote Leave less?
H0: No linear relationship between education share and Leave vote share.
Open regression-lecture.do and go to the Example section.

title: Lecture 8: Bivariate Regression
text:
Example: Step 1 — scatterplot
twoway (scatter leave_share share_high_skill) ///
       (lfit leave_share share_high_skill), leg(off)

Each dot is a UK region.
The line shows the estimated linear relationship.

title: Lecture 8: Bivariate Regression
text:
Example: Step 2 — run the regression
regress leave_share share_high_skill

Slope ≈ −1.13: each 1pp increase in education → 1.13pp less Leave.
95% CI: [−1.42, −0.84] — excludes zero → reject H0.
R-squared ≈ 0.30: education explains 30% of Leave vote variation.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
Today’s question

In Week 8 we found: import shock predicts Leave voting (slope = 28.38).
Could education or immigration be confounding that result?
We add controls one at a time and see what happens.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
section: Your Turn: Run the four models
text:
Your Turn: Run the four models

Run the do-file and look at the import shock coefficient across all four models.
How does the coefficient change as you add controls? Does it stay significant?
Discuss with your neighbour: what does the pattern tell you about confounding?

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
Model 1: Import shock alone
regress leave_share import_shock

Slope = 28.38: each unit of import shock predicts 28pp more Leave.
Significant (p < 0.001), R-squared = 0.14.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
Model 2: Adding immigrant share
regress leave_share import_shock immigrant_share

Import shock drops from 28.38 to 23.13 (still significant).
R-squared rises from 0.14 to 0.29.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
Model 3: Adding education instead
regress leave_share import_shock share_high_skill

Import shock drops from 28.38 to 12.85 (still significant, p = 0.006).
Education cuts the coefficient roughly in half.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
Model 4: Both controls together
regress leave_share import_shock immigrant_share share_high_skill

Import shock: 12.61 (p = 0.008), barely changes from Model 3.
Immigration adds almost nothing once education is controlled.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
Comparing the four models



Model
import_shock
p-value
R-squared

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
What does this tell us?

Education was a confound: it inflated import shock’s apparent effect.
But import shock survives the controls; the relationship appears genuine.
Controls make us more confident, but alone cannot prove causation.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
The limits of controls

We can only control for variables we observe and include.
Unobserved confounders could still bias the estimate.
How do researchers go further? One approach: instrumental variables.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
Colantone and Stanig (2018)

Studied the same question: does trade exposure cause support for Leave?
Used the same import shock measure from our dataset.
Concern: maybe UK import patterns reflect UK conditions, not just China’s rise.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
The instrumental variable idea

Find a variable that predicts import shock but is unrelated to UK confounders.
Their instrument: US import growth from China (same global shock, independent of UK).
Use only the part of UK import shock explained by the global trend.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
What did they find?

IV estimate was similar to the regression estimate with controls.
This suggests our regression is not badly biased by unobserved confounders.
IV gave them a stronger basis for a causal claim.

title: Lecture 10: Multivariate Regression
text:
Why this matters

Multivariate regression refines estimates but cannot prove causation alone.
Researchers use methods like DiD and IV to push closer to causal claims.
Data literacy means knowing what your tools can do and where they stop.

You’ll learn to


Distinguish descriptive and causal questions.
Explain what kind of claim each type of question supports.

Why care about this distinction?


Empirical questions can be descriptive or causal.
Descriptive questions ask what the world looks like.
Causal questions ask what would happen if we intervened.

Descriptive questions


Descriptive questions can be about distributions, trends, or correlations.

What percentage of countries are democratic?
Is there a global trend towards democratic backsliding?
Is democratic backsliding more prevalent in countries with higher political polarisation?



These questions are foundational for scientific research.

Causal questions


Causal questions ask if some variables drive change in others.

Does exposure to divisive content on social media make people more tolerant of political violence?
Does declining trust in political elites weaken commitment to democratic norms?
Do compulsory voting laws increase political participation?



These questions tell us what would happen under an intervention.

Distinction, not hierarchy


Causal questions are more directly concerned with what can be done to bring about social change.
But a prerequisite for changing the world is understanding what it looks like.
Causal and descriptive questions are equally important.

Complementarities between questions


Describing a distribution:

What percentage of the world’s wealth is held by the 50 richest people?

Describing a trend:

Is economic inequality increasing across the world?

Complementarities between questions


Describing a correlation:

Are autocracies more unequal than democracies?

Probing causation:

Do increases in income inequality make democratic backsliding more likely?

Recap


Empirical questions can be descriptive or causal.
Descriptive questions ask about distributions, trends, and correlations.
Causal questions ask about how some variables affect others.
Causal and descriptive questions complement each other to advance our scientific knowledge.

text:
You’ll learn to


Classify variables by type.
Evaluate how different types lead to different summaries.

Example: British Election Study, 2024


What is your age?
On a 0-10 scale, where 0 means left and 10 means right, where would you place yourself?
What is the highest qualification you have?
Which party did you vote for in the general election?

Age


What is your age?

Age


Answers are numeric quantities.
Has a true zero, and a 40-year-old is twice as old as a 20-year-old.
Age is a ratio variable.

Ratio variables


Ratio variables come in quantities that have a true zero.

Additional examples: A country’s GDP; A country’s population; A person’s income.

We can compute the mean and make mathematical operations with a ratio variable.

Eg., Dividing a country’s GDP by its population to compute the GDP per capita.

Ideology


On a 0-10 scale, where 0 means left and 10 means right, where would you place yourself?

Ideology


Answers are numeric quantities.
Does not have a true zero; a four does not mean “twice as much to the right” than a two.
Ideology is an interval variable.

Interval variables


Interval variables come in quantities that do not have a true zero.

Additional examples: Temperature (Celsius/Fahrenheit); a person’s credit score.

We can compute the mean of an interval variable, but cannot make certain mathematical operations with it.

Education level


What is the highest qualification you have?

Education level


Answers are categories (not quantities).
These categories are ordered.
The education level is an ordinal variable.

Ordinal variables


Ordinal variables come in categories that are ranked in a specific order.

Additional examples: How strongly a person agrees with a statement.

We can compute the means of certain ordinal variables, but interpreting them demands added caution.

General Election vote


Which party did you vote for in the general election?

General Election vote


Answers are categories (not quantities).
Categories cannot be ordered.
The General Election vote is a nominal variable.

Nominal variables


Nominal variables come in categories that cannot be ranked.

Additional examples: A person’s gender; a country’s electoral system type.

We cannot compute the mean or draw a histogram for a nominal variable.

Recap


Variables differ in the kind of information they carry.
The type of a variable constrains which summaries and comparisons make sense.

You’ll learn to


Interpret the variance and standard deviation as summaries of dispersion.

How good is 80%?


A university advertises that 80% of students are satisfied with the course.
But the national mean is about 82%.
With this new information, 80% is not as impressive as it seems.

Variance and standard deviation


The variance and standard deviation add context by informing us how spread out the distribution is.
This adds insight into how much an observation stands out from the rest.

Variance


The variance measures how far from the mean the observations tend to be.
The course with 80% approval rates is not too far from the mean.
But how about the others?

Calculating the variance


To get the variance, we start by subtracting the mean from each observation and squaring the difference.
Linguistics at the University of Glasgow has a 90% approval rate.
By subtracting the mean from this rate and squaring the difference, we get \((90-82)^2=8^2=64\)

Calculating the variance


We do this for every course and take the sum of the squared deviations for all courses.
By dividing this sum by the number of courses, we get the variance.
Courses that are further from the mean increase the variance of the distribution.

The variance formula

\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}\]

\(\mu\) is the mean.
\((x_i - \mu)^2\) is what we did earlier: \((90-82)^2\)
\(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\) means, “do this for every observation (\(x_i\)) and take the sum.”
We divide it by N to get the variance (\(\sigma^2\)).

The standard deviation


The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
More commonly used than the variance and useful to judge how unusual an observation is.
The variance for satisfaction with courses is about 145, and the standard deviation is about \(\sqrt{145}\approx12\).

Interpreting the standard deviation


Linguistics at Glasgow (90%) is two-thirds of a standard deviation above the mean: \(8/12=2/3\textrm{ s.d.}\)
Accounting at Strathclyde (94%) can be more boastful at one standard deviation above the mean: \(12/12=1\textrm{ s.d.}\)

Recap


Variance and standard deviation summarise how spread out a distribution is.
They are built by measuring how far observations are from the mean.

You’ll learn to


Define a population and a sample.
Explain how we use samples to draw conclusions about populations.
Explain why how data is collected affects what conclusions we can make.

section: We want to know about populations
text:
We want to know about populations


Once we have a research question and hypothesis, we want to collect data.
Ideally, we want data on every unit we are interested in.
The full set of units we want to draw conclusions about is called the population.

Populations depend on the question


The population is defined by who or what we are studying.

All voters in a general election.
All countries in the world.
All cities in the United Kingdom.



Populations do not have to be people — they are whatever units our question is about.

section: The problem: populations are often inaccessible
text:
The problem: populations are often inaccessible


Collecting data on every unit in a population is often too expensive or too slow.
Sometimes it is simply impossible.
We need a way to learn about the population without studying all of it.

The solution: samples


A sample is a subset of units drawn from the population.
We collect data on the sample and use it to reason about the population.
This is exactly what opinion polls do before an election.

From sample to population: inference


Drawing conclusions about a population using a sample is called inference.
But we can only make valid inferences from certain types of samples.
This is why how data is collected matters a lot.

Not all samples are equal


Imagine a news outlet that polls only its own viewers.
If viewers skew towards one political side, the sample will over-represent those views.
The sample will not look like the population — and any inference will be misleading.

Non-probability samples


In a non-probability sample, not every unit in the population has a chance of being selected.
These samples tend to be unrepresentative.
We cannot use non-probability samples to make valid inferences about the population.

Probability samples


In a probability sample, every unit in the population has a known chance of being selected.
The most important type is the simple random sample.
In a random sample, every unit has an equal probability of being chosen.

Why random samples are powerful


Random samples produce samples that are representative of the population.
The distribution of characteristics in the sample will closely mirror the population.
This allows us to generalise from the sample to the population with confidence.

Recap


A population is the full set of units we want to draw conclusions about.
A sample is a subset of the population that we actually observe.
Inference means using a sample to draw conclusions about a population.
Random samples are representative and support valid inference; non-probability samples do not.

Use a confidence interval to assess evidence against a null hypothesis.
Interpret results using the language of rejecting or failing to reject the null.
Explain what it means to fail to reject — and what it does not mean.

Where we left off


In the previous video, we built confidence intervals around point estimates.
A 95% confidence interval gives us a range of plausible values for the true population quantity.
Now we ask: can we use that interval to test a specific claim?

section: The null hypothesis as a claim about zero
text:
The null hypothesis as a claim about zero


A null hypothesis typically claims there is no difference between groups.
In other words, it claims the true difference is zero.
We can test this claim directly using a confidence interval.

The logic of the test


We construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference between groups.
Then we ask: does the interval include zero?

If zero is outside the interval: zero is not a plausible value for the true difference — we reject the null.
If zero is inside the interval: zero remains plausible — we fail to reject the null.

Example 1 — Gender and Reform vote


Research question: Are men more likely than women to vote for Reform?
Null hypothesis: There is no difference between men and women in their likelihood of voting Reform.
Alternative hypothesis: Men are more likely than women to vote for Reform.

Example 1 — The estimates

Example 1 — The test


The confidence interval for the difference is [0.7, 7.1].
The entire interval lies above zero.
Zero is not a plausible value for the true difference.
We reject the null hypothesis.

Example 2 — Newspaper readership and ideology


Research question: Do Daily Mail and Daily Telegraph readers differ in their political self-placement?
Null hypothesis: There is no difference in mean left-right self-placement between Mail and Telegraph readers.

section: What “fail to reject” does not mean
text:
What “fail to reject” does not mean


Failing to reject the null is not the same as proving the null is true.
We cannot conclude that Mail and Telegraph readers have identical ideologies.
It means the evidence in our sample is not strong enough to rule out zero.

Recap


A confidence interval can be used to test a null hypothesis.
If the 95% CI for a difference excludes zero, we reject the null hypothesis.
If it includes zero, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.
Failing to reject \(\neq\) confirming the null

text:
You’ll learn to


Recognise a regression equation as a linear function.
Read a scatterplot with a regression line.
Use a regression equation to generate predicted values.

Scatterplots and regression lines







Scatterplots show the relationship between two numeric variables.
That line is a regression line — and it comes from an equation.

Linear functions: the general form

\[y = a + bx\]

a is the intercept — the value of y when x = 0.
b is the slope — how much y changes per unit increase in x.

A simple example

\[y = 5 + 2x\]






Each value of x gives us a predicted value of y.

section: A regression equation is a linear function
text:
A regression equation is a linear function


Using data, we estimate the intercept and slope that best fit the observations.
The result is a linear equation — the same form as y = a + bx.
y is the dependent variable; x is the independent variable.

The Brexit example


Research question: Do areas with more graduates vote differently on Brexit?
y (dependent): Share of Leave votes (%)
x (independent): Share of population with higher education (%)
Education and Brexit

Reading the plot


Each dot is a UK region.
x-axis: share of the local population with higher education (2000).
y-axis: share of votes cast for Leave in the 2016 referendum.

Reading the plot


The regression line runs through the cloud of dots.
The line slopes downward: higher education share is associated with lower Leave vote.
This is the relationship the regression equation captures.

The regression equation

\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = 84 - 1.13 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

Intercept ≈ 84
Slope ≈ −1.13

Generating predictions

\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = 84 - 1.13 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

If HigherEd = 20%: 84 − 1.13(20) ≈ 61% Leave
If HigherEd = 30%: 84 − 1.13(30) ≈ 50% Leave

Predictions are approximations


Look at the scatter: not all regions with HigherEd = 20% voted 61% Leave.
Education is not the only factor that shapes the Leave vote.
The regression line summarises the average tendency, not every dot.

Recap


A regression equation is a linear function fitted to data.
It has an intercept (value of y when x = 0) and a slope (change in y per unit x).
We use it to generate predicted values of y for any value of x.

From description to inference

\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = 84 - 1.13 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

We estimated a slope of −1.13.
But could this reflect chance variation rather than a real relationship?
How do we test whether the slope is statistically significant?

section: Stating the hypothesis in regression terms
text:
Stating the hypothesis in regression terms

\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

Alternative hypothesis (H1): regions with more graduates voted Leave less.
In regression terms: \(\hat{\beta}_1 < 0\).

The null hypothesis

\[\widehat{\text{Leave}} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \times \text{HigherEd}\]

Null hypothesis (H0): education share is unrelated to Leave vote share.
In regression terms: \(\beta_1 = 0\).

What H0 = 0 means


If \(\beta_1 = 0\), the regression line is flat.
Higher education share would have no predictive value.
The apparent pattern in the data would be due to chance.

section: The significance test for the slope
text:
The significance test for the slope


We estimated \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -1.13\).
Is this far enough from zero to rule out chance?

The p-value for the slope


The p-value is the probability of observing a slope at least as extreme as −1.13 if the true slope were zero (i.e., if H0 were true).
A small p-value means the result is unlikely to be a chance finding.

The decision rule


Set significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\).
If p < 0.05 → reject H0; the slope is statistically significant.
If p > 0.05 → fail to reject H0.

Confidence intervals for the slope


We can also construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\hat{\beta}_1\).
If the CI does not include zero → reject H0.
If the CI includes zero → fail to reject H0.

Brexit results: applying the logic


Estimated slope: \(\hat{\beta}_1 = -1.13\) (negative, as H1 predicted).
95% CI for the slope: [-1.42, -0.84].
p-value is below 0.05.

Brexit results: the decision


We reject the null hypothesis.
Regions with higher education shares had a systematically lower Leave vote share.
The result is unlikely to reflect chance variation alone.

section: What makes a result more significant?
text:
What makes a result more significant?


Larger sample → smaller p-value.
Steeper slope (further from 0) → smaller p-value.
Less scatter around the regression line → smaller p-value.
Greater spread in x → smaller p-value.

Recap


H1 says \(\beta_1 \neq 0\); H0 says \(\beta_1 = 0\).
The p-value: probability of a slope at least as extreme as ours, if H0 were true.
A 95% CI excluding zero is equivalent to p < 0.05.

section: Health care spending and greenhouse gas emissions
text:
Health care spending and greenhouse gas emissions


Research Question: Does spending more in health care cause increases in greenhouse gas emissions?
Hypothesis: More health care spending causes greenhouse gas emissions to increase.
Hypothesis
Hypothesis
A positive correlation
A positive correlation
A confounding variable

Definition

A confounding variable:

Affects the dependent variable.
Affects the independent variable.
Is not a result of the independent variable.

Confounders vs. mediators


A confounder influences both X and Y from outside the relationship.
A mediator lies on the causal pathway from X to Y.
Mediators are part of the mechanism — not confounders.

An example of the distinction


Does education reduce crime? Possibly via higher income (mediator).
Higher income lies on the pathway: education → income → crime.
A confounder would affect both education and crime independently.

Omitted variable bias


When a confounder is left out of the analysis, estimates can mislead.
The relationship between X and Y may appear causal when it is not.
This is called omitted variable bias.

section: Omitted variable bias: the healthcare example
text:
Omitted variable bias: the healthcare example


National wealth is omitted → spending appears to cause emissions.
Once wealth is accounted for, the direct relationship may disappear.
This is why bivariate regression is often not enough.

Recap


A confounding variable affects both X and Y and is not caused by X.
Confounders create correlations that can look causal but are not.
Identifying confounders is essential before drawing causal conclusions.

text:
You’ll learn to


Explain the counterfactual problem in causal inference.
Describe how random assignment addresses confounding and reverse causality.
Identify the limits of experimental designs.

A causal question


Does exposure to misinformation online increase belief in conspiracy claims?
We observe a correlation: more exposure, more agreement with conspiracies.
But does exposure cause the beliefs — or is something else going on?

Problem 1: Reverse causality


People who already believe conspiracies may actively seek out misinformation.
The correlation may run from beliefs → exposure, not exposure → beliefs.
The causal direction is unclear from observational data alone.

Problem 2: Confounding variables


Political distrust, ideology, and education may influence both variables.
People with high distrust may be exposed to more misinformation and hold more conspiracy beliefs.
These confounders can make the relationship appear causal when it is not.

The counterfactual problem


Ideally, we would observe the same person in two states simultaneously.
One state: exposed to misinformation. One state: not exposed.
This is impossible — we can only observe what actually happened.

The logic of the counterfactual


We want to know: what would this person have believed without exposure?
That unobserved outcome is the counterfactual.
Causal inference is the problem of estimating it.

The experimental solution


Randomly assign participants to different information environments.
Treatment group: exposed to misinformation content.
Control group: exposed to neutral or factual content.

Why randomisation works


Random assignment makes the two groups similar on average.
Similar in distrust, ideology, education — and everything else.
Any difference in beliefs afterwards can be attributed to exposure itself.

What randomisation achieves


It breaks the link between exposure and pre-existing characteristics.
Confounders cannot be correlated with treatment if assignment is random.
Reverse causality cannot operate — exposure is imposed, not self-selected.

A brief note on ethics


Deliberately exposing participants to misinformation raises ethical concerns.
Researchers often use safeguards: simulated content, debriefing after the study.
Not all causal questions can be answered experimentally for ethical reasons.

When experiments are not possible


We cannot randomly assign people to years of education, war, or poverty.
Many important political questions involve variables that cannot be manipulated.
Other methods exist to approximate causal inference from observational data.

Recap


Random assignment creates comparable groups, isolating the effect of one variable.
It addresses both confounding and reverse causality simultaneously.
Where experiments are impossible, other tools are needed — and that is where statistics comes in.

text:
You’ll learn to


Explain why multivariate regression helps address confounding.
Interpret what happens when a coefficient “goes away.”
Recognise the limits of controlling for confounders.

Recall: Confounding variables


A confounding variable affects both X and Y, creating a spurious association.
We identified confounding as a threat to causal claims.
Multivariate regression lets us control for potential confounders.

How controlling works


Include the suspected confounder as a variable in the regression.
The coefficient on X now compares units with similar values of the confounder.
If X’s coefficient shrinks or disappears, confounding was likely present.

section: Example 1: Immigration and the Leave vote
text:
Example 1: Immigration and the Leave vote


Bivariate regression: regions with more immigrants voted Leave less.
Slope: \(b = -0.41\), statistically significant (\(p < 0.001\)).
But could education be driving both immigration and Leave voting?

Education as a confounder


Educated regions attract more immigrants (better economic opportunities).
Educated regions also voted Remain.
Education affects both the explanatory variable and the outcome.

Example 2: Health spending and CO2 emissions


Across countries, health expenditure strongly predicts CO2 emissions.
Slope: \(b = 0.73\) (\(p < 0.001\)). Countries spending more on health pollute more.
Does healthcare cause pollution? Obviously not. What is going on?

section: Does controlling for confounders prove causation?
text:
Does controlling for confounders prove causation?


No. “Confounding variables are everywhere.”
We can only control for variables we observe and think of.
Controls also do not address concerns about reverse causality.

Recap


Adding a confounder to a regression can reveal spurious relationships.
A coefficient that “goes away” suggests confounding was present.
Controls reduce confounding concerns but cannot establish causation.

Identify the parts of a publication-style regression table.
Read coefficients, standard errors, and significance stars.
Compare multiple models presented side by side.

Regressions “in the wild”


Regression tables in publications look different from software output.
They show multiple regressions in a single table.
This video teaches you how to read them.

The full table








This table shows three regressions predicting Leave vote share. Each column is a separate model. We will walk through each element.

Each column is a model








Column (1) regresses Leave share on education alone. Column (2) on immigration alone. Column (3) includes both. Each column is a complete regression.

The dependent variable








The dependent variable is shown at the top. All three models share the same dependent variable: Leave Vote Share (%).

Each row is a variable








The left side lists the independent variables: Higher Education, Immigrant Share, and the Constant (intercept). Each row shows how that variable relates to the dependent variable.

Blank cells








Some cells are blank. Model (1) has no immigration row because it only includes education. Model (2) has no education row. A blank cell means that variable was not included in that model.

Stars indicate significance








Stars are a shortcut for statistical significance. Three stars (***) means p < 0.01. The note at the bottom of the table defines the thresholds. Notice that immigration in Model (3) has no stars: it is not statistically significant once education is controlled for.

Standard errors








The numbers in parentheses below each coefficient are standard errors. They measure how precisely the coefficient is estimated. Smaller standard errors mean more precise estimates.

The bottom panel








The bottom of the table shows summary statistics for each model: the number of observations and R-squared. These help you assess sample size and how much variation the model explains.

Recap


Each column is a separate regression model.
Stars indicate significance; parentheses contain standard errors.
Comparing columns reveals how coefficients change across models.

section: Read through the do-file comments and execute the commands
text:
Read through the do-file comments and execute the commands

This do-file will serve as your companion for learning how to run hypothesis tests in Stata.
The do-file covers two tests: a difference in proportions and a difference in means.

From description to inference

Last week: cross-tabulations, bar charts of means, scatterplots.
This week: could the patterns we observed be due to chance variation alone?

Test 1: Difference in proportions

Research question: Are countries with a British colonial history more likely to be democracies today than countries with a French colonial history?
Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no systematic difference between British- and French-colonised countries in their likelihood of being democracies.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Countries with a British colonial history are more likely to be democratic than countries with a French colonial history.

Cross-tabulation
keep if ht_colonial == 5 | ht_colonial == 6

tabulate ht_colonial bmr_dem, row nofreq

This restricts the data to British (5) and French (6) colonised countries.
The row percentages show the share of democracies in each group.
These are the proportions the test will compare.

Run the test

prtest compares the proportion of a binary variable across two groups.

prtest bmr_dem, by(ht_colonial)

bmr_dem is already coded 0 (non-democracy) and 1 (democracy) — no recoding needed.
Stata will compare the proportion of 1s (democracies) in each group.

Reading the output







Element
What it tells you




Proportion 1 / Proportion 2
Share of democracies in each group


diff
Estimated gap (Group 1 − Group 2)


95% Conf. Interval for diff
Range of plausible values for the true gap


Pr(|Z| > |z|)
p-value: probability of this gap if H0 were true

The decision rule

Focus on the 95% confidence interval for the difference.
Ask: does the interval include zero?




CI for the difference
Decision




Does not include 0
Reject the null hypothesis


Includes 0
Fail to reject the null hypothesis

Test 2: Difference in means

Research question: Is turnout higher in countries with proportional systems than in countries with majoritarian systems?
Null Hypothesis (H0): Mean voter turnout is the same in majoritarian and proportional electoral systems.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Proportional systems have higher turnout than majoritarian systems.

section: Before moving on: reload the dataset
text:
Before moving on: reload the dataset
use "data-raw/Quality_of_Government_2026.dta", clear

Earlier on, we ran a command to only keep countries that were British or French colonies.
Reload so we can have the full dataset again.

Compare means
keep if gol_est == 1 | gol_est == 2

by gol_est, sort: summarize ideavt_legvt

This restricts the data to majoritarian (1) and proportional (2) systems.
Mixed systems (3) are excluded — we are comparing the two pure types.

Run the test

ttest compares the mean of a continuous variable across two groups.

ttest ideavt_legvt, by(gol_est)

ideavt_legvt is the percentage of the voting-age population that cast a vote.
Stata will compare the mean turnout in each electoral system type.

Reading the output







Element
What it tells you




Mean
Average turnout in each group


diff
Estimated gap (Group 1 − Group 2)


95% Conf. Interval for diff
Range of plausible values for the true gap


Pr(|T| > |t|)
p-value: probability of this gap if H0 were true

The decision rule

Focus on the 95% confidence interval for the difference.
Ask: does the interval include zero?




CI for the difference
Decision




Does not include 0
Reject the null hypothesis


Includes 0
Fail to reject the null hypothesis

Recap

prtest tests whether two groups differ in their proportion of a binary outcome.
ttest tests whether two groups differ in their mean of a continuous outcome.
Both tests produce a difference, a confidence interval, and a p-value.
If the 95% CI for the difference excludes zero, reject the null hypothesis.

title: Hypothesis Testing in Stata
text:
Run a difference-in-proportions test in Stata.
Run a difference-in-means test in Stata.
Read the output and apply the confidence interval decision rule.








Access our Shared Project Folder
Click on data-raw
Download Quality_of_Government_2026.dta
Save it into the data-raw folder on your computer








Access our Shared Project Folder
Click on do
Download hypothesis-qog.do
Save it into the do folder on your computer








Set the working directory to your project folder on your computer.
Load the dataset

cd "C:\Users\leona\OneDrive - King's College London\shared-project-folder"

use "data-raw/Quality_of_Government_2026.dta", clear







This do-file will serve as your companion for learning how to run hypothesis tests in Stata.
The do-file covers two tests: a difference in proportions and a difference in means.








Last week: cross-tabulations, bar charts of means, scatterplots.
This week: could the patterns we observed be due to chance variation alone?








Research question: Are countries with a British colonial history more likely to be democracies today than countries with a French colonial history?
Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no systematic difference between British- and French-colonised countries in their likelihood of being democracies.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Countries with a British colonial history are more likely to be democratic than countries with a French colonial history.







keep if ht_colonial == 5 | ht_colonial == 6

tabulate ht_colonial bmr_dem, row nofreq

This restricts the data to British (5) and French (6) colonised countries.
The row percentages show the share of democracies in each group.
These are the proportions the test will compare.








prtest compares the proportion of a binary variable across two groups.

prtest bmr_dem, by(ht_colonial)

bmr_dem is already coded 0 (non-democracy) and 1 (democracy) — no recoding needed.
Stata will compare the proportion of 1s (democracies) in each group.














Element
What it tells you




Proportion 1 / Proportion 2
Share of democracies in each group


diff
Estimated gap (Group 1 − Group 2)


95% Conf. Interval for diff
Range of plausible values for the true gap


Pr(|Z| > |z|)
p-value: probability of this gap if H0 were true










Focus on the 95% confidence interval for the difference.
Ask: does the interval include zero?




CI for the difference
Decision




Does not include 0
Reject the null hypothesis


Includes 0
Fail to reject the null hypothesis










Research question: Is turnout higher in countries with proportional systems than in countries with majoritarian systems?
Null Hypothesis (H0): Mean voter turnout is the same in majoritarian and proportional electoral systems.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Proportional systems have higher turnout than majoritarian systems.







use "data-raw/Quality_of_Government_2026.dta", clear

Earlier on, we ran a command to only keep countries that were British or French colonies.
Reload so we can have the full dataset again.







keep if gol_est == 1 | gol_est == 2

by gol_est, sort: summarize ideavt_legvt

This restricts the data to majoritarian (1) and proportional (2) systems.
Mixed systems (3) are excluded — we are comparing the two pure types.








ttest compares the mean of a continuous variable across two groups.

ttest ideavt_legvt, by(gol_est)

ideavt_legvt is the percentage of the voting-age population that cast a vote.
Stata will compare the mean turnout in each electoral system type.














Element
What it tells you




Mean
Average turnout in each group


diff
Estimated gap (Group 1 − Group 2)


95% Conf. Interval for diff
Range of plausible values for the true gap


Pr(|T| > |t|)
p-value: probability of this gap if H0 were true










Focus on the 95% confidence interval for the difference.
Ask: does the interval include zero?




CI for the difference
Decision




Does not include 0
Reject the null hypothesis


Includes 0
Fail to reject the null hypothesis










prtest tests whether two groups differ in their proportion of a binary outcome.
ttest tests whether two groups differ in their mean of a continuous outcome.
Both tests produce a difference, a confidence interval, and a p-value.
If the 95% CI for the difference excludes zero, reject the null hypothesis.



Why this matters:

Descriptive analysis tells us what patterns look like in our data.
Hypothesis testing tells us whether those patterns are too large to dismiss as chance variation.
These two commands — prtest and ttest — are the building blocks for statistical inference in political science research.

text:
You’ll learn to

Recode invalid values to missing using replace.
Drop observations based on a condition.
Generate a binary variable from a logical statement.
Save a cleaned dataset as a separate file.

section: Download the companion do-file for this activity
text:
Download the companion do-file for this activity

Access our Shared Project Folder
Click on do
Download prepare-bes.do
Save it into the do folder on your computer

Why data preparation matters

Raw data may contain invalid or missing value codes.
Analysing uncleaned data can produce incorrect results.
A short preparation step before analysis prevents these errors.

An important preamble

Data preparation is not always necessary! Depending on the data you choose, analysing raw data may work.
Don’t apply these examples to your case without considering whether you need them.
You should learn to determine when data preparation is needed and what commands to use (but you can always ask for help).

Missing values in Stata

In Stata, . represents a missing value.
Survey datasets often encode missing responses as negative numbers.
These must be recoded to . before analysis.

section: Operation 1: Recode invalid values to missing
text:
Operation 1: Recode invalid values to missing
replace age = . if age < 0

Any observation where age is negative gets recoded to missing.
Stata will then exclude these observations from calculations automatically.
Repeat for each variable that uses negative codes for missing data.

section: Operation 2: Drop observations based on a condition
text:
Operation 2: Drop observations based on a condition
drop if k03 != 7 & k03 != 13

Removes all observations that are neither Mail nor Telegraph readers.
Restricts the sample to the two groups being compared.
Use drop if whenever analysis requires a specific subgroup only.

The equivalent using keep if
keep if k03 == 7 | k03 == 13

Keeps only Mail (7) or Telegraph (13) readers — same result.
drop if and keep if are logical mirror images of each other.
Use whichever makes the intended restriction easier to read.

Operation 3: Generate a binary variable
gen voted_reform = (b02 == 8) if b02 != .

The expression (b02 == 8) returns 1 if true, 0 if false.
The condition if b02 != . ensures missing values are not assigned a code.
Use when you need to reclassify multiple categories into two.

Labelling the new variable
label define reform_lbl 1 "Reform" 0 "Another Party"
label values voted_reform reform_lbl

label define creates a set of value labels.
label values attaches them to the variable.
Labels make output easier to read without changing underlying values.

Operation 4 (Optional): Save the cleaned dataset
save "data-clean/bes_clean.dta", replace

Save the cleaned file to a separate folder from the raw data.
Never overwrite raw data — keep it as originally downloaded.
The replace option overwrites any previous version of the clean file.

Recap

replace x = . if x < 0 — recode invalid values to missing.
drop if condition — remove observations outside the subgroup of interest.
generate with a logical statement — create a binary variable.
Save cleaned data to a separate folder; never overwrite raw data.
